inline.s: Instruction to the Chan Monks Huimiao and Xinghou

In the land of the Eastern Sea the Buddhadharma does not flourish. Since Master Guifeng of Lingshan began to teach and convert there, no small number have been led to forsake the crooked and return to the upright. In former days the old man dwelt at Haiyin Temple and marveled at how richly that master's Dharma benefited others; most of his disciples were able to expound the Dharma. The student Xinghou of today is his direct heir. It is now twenty-eight years since the old man left Lingshan. In the year xinyou he came to seek instruction at Mount Kuang; after the turn of the year he took his leave to return to his old mountain, asking for the essentials of cultivating the mind. The old man therefore instructed him, saying: What the Buddha censures above all are the two obstructions, that of afflictions and that of the knowable, for they are the root of birth and death. The obstruction of afflictions is greed, anger, delusion and craving, the root of birth and death for ordinary people. The obstruction of the knowable is the knowledge and views of Buddhadharma, the root of birth and death for the sages of the three vehicles. If these two obstructions are not removed, there is no way to escape the mass of suffering. Alas, among the people of today those who do not know the Buddhadharma are hardly to be blamed; but even those who study the Buddhadharma do not cut off afflictions, and instead make the Dharma they have learned into an obstruction of the knowable, fostering arrogance and heaping up further afflictions. Their minds are defiled; the seeds are triggered and burst into activity, and they let themselves go. Body and mind are utterly unrestrained, and they follow their feelings in creating karma. Is this not a great error? Now that you, student, have heard the old man's instruction and know that this is the great matter of birth and death, you have aroused the mind to inquire and seek and to work at the ground of your own nature; this is the most excellent power of vow. Yet in your inquiry you need not seek anything else. Simply sweep clean, one by one, all the old seeds of habit in your breast, and permit none of them to burst into activity. In daily life, wherever you meet objects and conditions, at the very place where a thought arises, see through it on the spot and allow no continuation. As for the way to apply the mind, take the Śūraṅgama Sūtra's account of Guanyin's perfect penetration through the ear-faculty: turning the mechanism of hearing around, one hears back into one's own nature. This single gate of contemplation is the best way to apply the mind. If in daily seeing and hearing you can truly look back upon your own nature, you will not be carried along by outer objects. Turning the stream back thought after thought, every thought is a road home to the real. Apply the mind thus, yet if habits are not removed and burst into activity, your effort will surely lack power. All of it rests on this one point of turning against present karma, which is the highest practice. But you must also have a keen mind for birth and death; only then will you be willing to put in deadly earnest effort. Only when you truly work at it for the sake of birth and death will you have any benefit. It is not a matter of hearing it and letting it go, turning it into one more item of Buddhist knowledge and views.
Instruction to the Layman Jingxin

Formerly, when the old man passed through Wuzhong, the layman Jingxin came to pay his respects and ask for instruction, and the old man taught him the method of Buddha-recitation. Recitation is like the clear-water pearl that can purify muddy water; hence he was given the style-name Pure Mind. Several years have passed since we parted. Now he writes that his recitation finds it hard to become a single piece, and again asks for instruction. The old man therefore said: In practice the first requirement is a keen mind for birth and death. If the mind for birth and death is not keen, how dare one speak of recitation becoming a single piece? Moreover, through measureless kalpas beings have thought deluded thoughts moment by moment, their roots of craving firmly covered. Even in this present life, when has a single thought been painfully set on birth and death? Day by day, thought after thought follows feeling, and never once do they turn back and reflect. Now you wish, with a shallow and drifting faith, to cut off the birth and death of many kalpas; that is what is called saving a pile of firewood with a drop of water. How could such a principle hold? If your mind for birth and death were truly keen, every thought would be like putting out a fire on your own head; you would only fear that, once this human body is lost, a hundred kalpas may not restore it. You must clench this one recitation of the Buddha's name and resolve to stand against your deluded thoughts, so that all suffering stands present before you and is not screened off by delusion. Laboring thus with bitter earnestness, in time it becomes pure and familiar and naturally responds. Then, without seeking a single piece, it becomes a single piece of itself. This matter is like drinking water: cold and warm are known only to oneself and cannot be told to another. Everything depends on your own effort. If you merely make recitation a mask for your face, you will never in the year of the donkey have any benefit. You must be brave and fierce, and hesitate no longer.
Instruction to the Elder Rentian on Holding the Lotus Sūtra

The Great Virtue Rentian had recited the Lotus Sūtra for more than twenty years. As he was about to set out he asked for instruction, and the old man said to him: The Lotus is the Supreme Vehicle, the essential secret long guarded by our Buddha, and the writ of assurance by which he conferred on his disciples the prophecy of buddhahood. The Sixth Patriarch said: When the mind is deluded, the Lotus turns the mind; when the mind is awake, the mind turns the Lotus. To recite the sutra without understanding its meaning is to make an enemy of its sense. The Twenty-Seventh Patriarch said: The in-breath does not dwell in the realm of the aggregates; the out-breath does not touch any condition. Thus one constantly turns such a sutra, hundreds of thousands of millions of scrolls. Given what these two patriarchs said, how after all does Rentian hold this sutra? The sutra says: This Dharma cannot be understood by thought and discrimination. If so, then even the Sixth Patriarch, granting that he understood its meaning, still could not be said to hold it. Again it says: This sutra opens the gate of expedient means in order to reveal the true mark of all dharmas. If so, then mountains, rivers and the great earth, grasses, trees, tiles and stones are none of them other than the true mark; and even the Twenty-Seventh Patriarch, apart from in-breath and out-breath, still could not be said to hold it. Then how, after all, does Rentian hold it? As the Buddha said in the chapter on Holding the Sutra, even the fiftieth person in succession who transmits the teaching and has others hold the sutra gains merit beyond conception. From this we see that the merit of transmitting the teaching does not depend on whether one understands the meaning or not, nor on whether one is free of breath or not; one need only have a single thought of faith and know for oneself what is originally possessed, and the wisdom-life is not cut off. Therefore the old man praises the Blue Lotus Dharma Society above all, taking the holding of the Lotus as a wondrous practice. For as soon as one hears this sutra, one plants the true seed of buddhahood. If Rentian transmits this teaching to many people, as the Buddha praised, what other dharma could surpass it?
Instruction to Shen Dajie

Chan and Pure Land, these two practices, are from the outset not two dharmas; Master Yongming demonstrated this long ago. Chan is essentially free of thought — so be it. Yet the Pure Land has the highest grade of the highest rebirth, and that is never attained otherwise than by cultivation within freedom from thought. If one speaks of reciting the Buddha's name to the point of single-mindedness without distraction, is any thought retained there? Still, although in this there is no duality, when it comes to the actual work of application there is no lack of skill and clumsiness. For in inquiry the place where the mind is applied is most subtle and most close. When one is engaged in inquiry, it is a matter of not giving rise to a single thought; but if one speaks of reciting the Buddha's name, then a thought does arise. Thus there do seem to be two separate pieces. One must take the point of inquiry and the point of recitation and beat them into one line, so that what does not arise yet arises, and what arises is itself non-arising. Only this is the true practice of Yongjia's brightness and stillness flowing together. Why? If one discusses inquiry as the raising of a huatou, blocking off the root of the intellect so that not one thought arises, this is indeed the work of inquiry; but the ancients called it hugging the post while rowing the oar. That very thought of wanting no thought to arise is itself an arising; how could it be true non-arising? It is the same with recitation: if you hang the Buddha's name in your heart and never forget it thought after thought, how is that true single-mindedness without distraction? The ancients taught people to inquire into the living phrase, not the dead phrase; the very point is, in the midst of arising, to see the meaning of non-arising. As the sutra says: One who sees the instant awakens to non-arising. By this one saying, inquiry and recitation can at once become a single line. Practitioner, listen closely: in inquiring while reciting, it is easy to fall into confusion and error — do not take it lightly. How is inquiry itself recitation, and recitation itself inquiry? In your inquiry now, simply take the single phrase Amitābha as your huatou and do the work of examining it thoroughly. Put down all at once your own body, mind and world, together with all your former worldly conventions, habitual talk, and Buddhist knowledge and views. Then, from within emptiness and stillness, muster your strength and raise up one invocation of Amitābha Buddha, clear and distinct. Just as you raise it, look straight down at it and examine thoroughly: who is it that recites the Buddha's name? Bring up doubt again; examine and examine again, doubt and doubt again. Like a donkey gazing into a well, gaze on and on, doubt on and on, until you reach the place where the road of thought is cut off, like a silver mountain and an iron wall, with no place to turn the body or draw breath. Then suddenly you knock against it, touch it — the very meaning of non-arising — and it bursts forth before you; your whole body streams with sweat, as if waking from a great dream. Only then will you believe that arising is non-arising and non-arising is arising, that inquiry is recitation and recitation is inquiry. Looking back, you will know that all along you were like one searching for Chang'an while inside the Hanyuan Hall. In doing this work, the thing most to be feared is a mind that wants to awaken. The moment there is a mind that wants to awaken, that is a plank across your head. Just keep working straight on, with no reckoning of the schedule. When you reach the point where you cannot go on, rouse your spirits and start afresh. And you must never crave the mysterious and wonderful. Even if a thought subsides for a while and you feel still and joyful, never take that as something good; you must spit it out. Never take the mysterious sayings and wondrous words of the buddhas and patriarchs as your proof and call them Buddhadharma. Nor may you fall into the armor of do-nothingness and take that as attainment. In short, pay no heed to saint or ordinary being, delusion or awakening; single-mindedly seek where one thought comes to rest. Pursue it until it is hunted down and utterly cut off, and in time you will see your original face — like meeting your own father at the crossroads: you will not ask anyone where he is. Seen thus, this matter is from the beginning each person's own business, with nothing especially marvelous about it. If you, practitioner, would truly take the great matter of birth and death to heart, try starting from here; you will certainly not be cheated.

Instruction to the Chan Monk Benhuaiyin

Long ago, at the assembly on Vulture Peak, our Buddha wished to entrust the Wondrous Lotus Sūtra to someone, charging him to uphold it in the final age and spread it abroad. Never mind the hundreds of thousands of gods and humans who received the prophecy of buddhahood; among all his disciples there was not one who dared to circulate this Dharma in the Sahā world. It had to wait for the host of bodhisattvas sprung from the earth before it could be shouldered. Is the holding of this Dharma so very easy? Because in the evil world of the five turbidities beings have scant merit and their natures are hard and violent, the most difficult of all to tame, our Buddha taught those who hold the sutra that patience must be the first practice. Hence he said: After the Tathāgata's extinction, one who wishes to expound this sutra to the four assemblies should enter the Tathāgata's chamber, put on the Tathāgata's robe, and sit on the Tathāgata's seat; then he may widely expound this sutra for the assembly. The Tathāgata's chamber is the mind of great compassion amid all living beings. The Tathāgata's robe is the mind of gentleness and patience. The Tathāgata's seat is the emptiness of all dharmas. Dwelling securely in these, and then with a mind free of indolence, one may expound the Lotus Sūtra for the assembly. Thus the Buddha recounted his own past practice in seeking the Dharma: how Devadatta in life after life wronged him, and how Never-Disparaging paid homage, and how the four assemblies even reviled him, or attacked him with knives, sticks, tiles and stones — all such sufferings he endured with joy, without one thought of indolence or retreat. This is precisely the Dharma taught to bodhisattvas, the supreme practice of holding the sutra in the final age. We who are sons of the Buddha — if we have no practice of patience, how shall we hold the Buddha's wisdom-life and keep it unbroken? And when he entrusted the sutra to the bodhisattvas who would hold it, he made them vow: All kinds of suffering we shall be able to endure. Therefore the Buddha said that if one surveys the three thousand great thousand worlds, there is not so much as a mustard seed's worth of space that is not a place where a bodhisattva gave up body and life in quest of bodhi; even head, eyes, marrow and brain were not spared. So he taught those who hold the sutra to begin with the practice of patience. Alas for this Dharma-ending age: without great power of patience, how can one protect the Buddhadharma and continue the wisdom-life? The old man has again and again expounded the practice of patience to Chan monks. This monk was able to believe the old man deeply and has sustained himself by the power of patience; now he has not only preserved the monastery to the end, but has also perfected his own practice. He must never be judged by ordinary worldly standards, nor should one seek the Dharma of birth and death anywhere apart from this. Moreover, this sutra is the one great cause for which our Buddha, the World-Honored One, appeared in the world. The one great cause is the Buddha's knowledge and vision, which beings inherently possess. The Buddha's knowledge and vision means the ability to see the true mark of all dharmas. Because beings are deluded as to the true knowledge and vision, they merely identify with the illusory and false body and mind of the five aggregates and do not see the true mark. If one sees the true mark, then throughout the three realms above and below there is not a single dharma to be found; where then could birth and death lodge? If this is so, can it be that only Chan inquiry can end birth and death, while holding the sutra cannot? Nanyue and Tiantai were both great patriarchs who awakened to the true mark. If among the companions of the Dharma Society who read and recite this sutra there should be even one who awakens and enters the Lotus samādhi as Tiantai did, then this very assembly on Vulture Peak is solemnly present and has never dispersed. Those who protect and uphold it will then be replete with Ganges-sands merit beyond conception. For this Dharma the Buddha, kalpa after kalpa, life after life, gave up body and life. If this monk can give up this one life and accomplish a great Dharma-benefit, why look outside and seek the Buddhadharma elsewhere? Even if today one cannot end birth and death, if one relies on this Dharma as a boat, upholding it with the power of vow, then in the sea of birth and death one will surely in the end reach the other shore; that is better than the former life of living in vain and dying in vain. Since this monk believes the old man's words, let him from now on rouse a great power of patience and a great power of diligence; this is called truly offering the Dharma to the Tathāgata and fulfilling Samantabhadra's great practice. Never give rise to a mind of arising and ceasing, set up views of self and others, and so conceive the thought of retreating and falling away.
Instruction to the Chan Monk Benyuanjue of Yangshan in Xin'an

Benyuanjue restored the Yangshan monastery over more than thirty years; the many splendors that appeared there like a conjuration all came from the power of his own mind. He also recited the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment and the Sutra of Brahma Conduct for more than twenty years, maintaining pure conduct with care; all this came from prajñā habituated in past lives. Now he came to pay homage at Mount Kuang, asked to receive the great precepts, and, holding up incense, requested an exposition of the great purport of the Perfect Enlightenment. The old man therefore instructed him, saying: The Buddha taught that all dharmas above and below the three realms are made by the one mind alone. It is said that from perfect enlightenment flow all pure true suchness, bodhi, nirvāṇa and the pāramitās, for the instruction of bodhisattvas. Therefore, as a son of the Buddha, if one penetrates the gate of mind-only, then all causes and results, defiled and pure, are right here before one and transform with every thought. Hence it is said: When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure. Take the case of Yangshan: it was once all dangerous cliffs and craggy rocks, wild thickets and rank grass; now in a single day this monastery has appeared there as though fallen from heaven. All of it came from the first thought of firm faith, and so brought about such vast Buddhist work. From this we see that the Western Pure Land, too, is hardly to be obtained apart from the mind. Today the old man specially confers on this monk the Brahmā Net Vajra Jewel Precepts. These precepts are called Vairocana's gate of the mind-ground. The sutra says: If one receives the Buddha's precepts, one immediately enters the rank of the buddhas. Know therefore that a single thought of faith at once opens the Buddha's knowledge and vision, and all Buddha-lands appear before that thought. Hence all buddhas' Pure Lands are established from the vajra mind-ground. If this monk can truly understand this gate, then from now on, in every daily activity, clearly knowing that all is poured out from his own mind, each dharma will be a true cause of the Pure Land. If he can further hold the one invocation Amitābha Buddha, never forgetting it, never dulling it, reciting until movement and stillness are not two and waking and sleeping are as one, then every step before him treads the Pure Land; walking in procession on jeweled ground, this very body and mind already sits within the lotus calyx. When the time of death comes and he lets go this body, the flower will open and he will see the Buddha, as if waking from a dream. Only then will he know that birth and death are a dream and the Pure Land a conjuration, and in a single thought he will dwell forever in the stage of non-retrogression. What dharma besides this can deliver one from birth and death? This monk has long cultivated pure conduct, but he has not yet heard a good teacher in person to shatter the dream of former deluded thoughts. He has only to understand that every dharma is mind-only; what need is there to seek the Buddhadharma elsewhere? Strive on, and take care.
Instruction to the Good Man Chen

Chu and Mian are renowned prefectures, lands of ancient culture; yet teachers of the Dharma who have passed through and transformed them are rare. The Chan monk Guanzhi planted his staff here and kept retreat for three years, and for a time many turned to him. The good man who has lately come is an old disciple who took refuge in faith. He came from afar to consult the old man of Mount Kuang and asked for instruction to pass on to the people. The old man therefore instructed him, saying: Men and women in the household who can keep the five precepts — not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct, not speaking falsely, and not drinking wine or eating meat — when the Buddha was in the world, such people were always called upāsaka and upāsikā in the assemblies. This means near-serving men and women, because they are fit to draw near and serve the Three Jewels. What they practice is the careful keeping of the five precepts, by which they avoid falling into the three evil paths; this is the blessing of gods and humans. Hence it is said: If the five precepts are not kept, the road to the heavens and the human realm is cut off. In keeping the five precepts, the first thing is to understand and believe in cause and effect: good and evil retribution follow like shadow to form. Doing good creates a cause of blessing whose fruit is surely rebirth among gods or humans; creating evil brings an evil fruit, and one must fall into the three evil paths. Consider the high officials and noble ranks of the world, the rich and honored — such people must have cultivated blessings in former lives: offering to the Three Jewels, feeding monks, giving alms, printing sutras, making images, building temples and pagodas, relieving the poor and rescuing the suffering. Their long life and many sons, fathers kind and sons filial, husband leading and wife following, elder brothers friendly and younger respectful — all this must come from releasing living beings, not killing, and keeping fasts and precepts. If a householder can keep these five precepts, the five constant virtues are complete in him: not killing is benevolence; not stealing is righteousness; not committing sexual misconduct is propriety; not speaking falsely is trustworthiness; not drinking wine is wisdom. One who can do this in the Confucian school is a gentleman of accomplished virtue. How could keeping a fast be a matter outside one's duty? Among such people there are those of high intelligence and lofty understanding who, having kept these precepts, further reflect that the human world is impermanent, like a candle in the wind, and fear that once this human body is lost, ten thousand kalpas may not restore it. Reflecting thus and pondering the suffering of birth and death, their mind of renunciation grows keen; they should then arouse the mind to hold and recite Amitābha Buddha. Lay this one Buddha across your heart, never breaking it thought after thought, never forgetting it moment after moment; morning and evening bow to the Buddha and recite sutras, dedicating the merit toward the West and seeking rebirth in the Pure Land. If recitation becomes pure and familiar and the mind is single without distraction, then at the time of death one will see Amitābha Buddha send forth light to receive and guide one; one will be received into a lotus and take it as one's father and mother. When the flower opens one sees the Buddha, and from then on one is forever freed from the suffering of birth and death and turning in the wheel; one takes final leave of the three realms. Such a one is called a bodhisattva. This work of recitation has been practiced by men and women in households in every age, accomplished in a single life, and many have been born in the West. Hence it is said: There is only the direct path of practice — simply recite Amitābha Buddha. To seek anything else is deviant view and deviant conduct. If the good man holds this and converts others of his kind, then one person, one family, and on to one village, one prefecture, one whole city, will become a Buddha-land. Only strive in your practice; if your faith is true and keen and you carry it out with a single thought, you need not seek any other wondrous Buddhadharma.
Instruction to Sheng Liansheng

Laozi said: My great affliction is that I have a body. If I had no body, what affliction would I have? The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: This body of mine is composed of the four great elements. One should contemplate that within the body hardness returns to earth, moisture to water, warmth to fire, and movement to wind. When the four elements each separate, where then is this false body? Contemplating thus in earnest, in time the mind becomes wholly familiar with it and the mark of the body suddenly becomes empty. All kinds of afflictions arise from deluded and inverted thought; like the inversions of a dream, they were never really there. When affliction arises, look directly at this mind's deluded thought: where does it arise from? Pursue it to the place where it was never born, and deluded thought no longer arises. When deluded thought does not arise, affliction is empty. When body and mind are suddenly empty, all afflictions are at once extinguished, and with that thought one enters the cool land of ultimate bliss. This contemplation is of the essence; it is the wondrous medicine for escaping suffering. Yet for a beginner the contemplation is not easily accomplished. Simply take Amitābha Buddha as your huatou and examine it truly, never letting it go. When a deluded thought arises, raise the huatou and press it — the deluded thought will vanish of itself. Because ordinarily you have no right mindfulness, you follow deluded thoughts wholly and are carried along, clinging without pause and so feeding your suffering. All dharmas arise from the mind; outside the mind there are no dharmas. If one does not contemplate the mind but seeks a road of escape from suffering, it is like stepping backward and hoping to go forward. You need only rouse a brave and fierce mind; never say you cannot — that is drawing your own limits.
Instruction to Wu Qigao

Qigao had long taken refuge in the Three Jewels and had kept a vegetarian mind for years. Now he came to Mount Kuang to seek the conferring of the precepts and to become a disciple of the Dharma gate, so as to form a bond for future transcendence. He was therefore given the name Fuchang and the style-name Layman Pure Mind, and the upāsaka precepts were conferred on him. Again he held up incense and asked for instruction. The old man therefore said: All the various karma-activities of the world are impermanent and are wholly causes of suffering; hence beings are born in the Sahā land, a place where beings are gathered, which is why it is called Endurance. Foolish and deluded people take suffering for joy, and so increase craving and add further to the root of suffering, not knowing what is essential for escaping it — this is inversion. Therefore, if anyone in the whole world has but a single thought recognizing that all is impermanent, suffering and empty, and arouses the mind to seek transcendence, that person is a person of great wisdom. If he has but a single thought of turning back and reflecting, arousing a mind that wearies of suffering, that is the road out of suffering. If he has but a single thought of the vow to seek rebirth in the Pure Land, that is the root of buddhahood. This is why the Buddha taught the precepts, instructing people to stop evil and cultivate good: when evil is stopped the mind is pure; when good is cultivated suffering ceases. When suffering ceases blessing increases. A pure mind is the cause of the Pure Land; the ending of suffering is the root of ultimate bliss; the increase of blessing is the fruit of everlasting joy. Know therefore that a single thought of resolving to receive the precepts can cut off the mass of suffering, gather the mass of blessings, bring one out of birth and death, and win rebirth in the Pure Land — all from that first thought of resolve, which is the causal ground. Since the layman today can know this matter and arouse this mind, then whatever he does is a transcendent act. Though not yet a monk, he is already named a son of the Buddha. From now on, if he truly recites the Buddha's name with the mind that keeps the precepts, purifying away the long-standing defilements of greed, anger, delusion and craving and all the afflictions of the mind, his mind-ground will be pure. Reciting the Buddha's name with this pure mind, never forgetting it, never breaking it, then every matter before him in daily life is a cause of the Pure Land, and all his giving — the four kinds of offering to the Three Jewels — is provision for adorning the Pure Land. It is as said: When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure; the Pure Land is mind-only, and the Amitābha of one's own nature is from the first not apart from this person's single thought. This is true Dharma-practice, and this is what is meant by the blessing of true permanence arising from a pure mind. If the layman can truly believe without doubt, what need is there to seek the Buddhadharma elsewhere? Only he must not regard this as an ordinary worldly matter; if he does not, his resolve for the Way will firm itself and his faith will grow day by day. Take care, take care.
Instruction to the Chan Monk Wuzhi Jian

One who leaves the household life must first understand that leaving home, cutting off affection and taking leave of kin, is fundamentally for the sake of escaping birth and death. If it is for the great matter of birth and death, one must know that all dharmas of the world are the root of suffering and that the body is a mass of suffering; one must certainly arouse the mind to practice and seek the way out of suffering. First one must see through the present state of body and mind. Contemplate that this body is a form falsely compounded of the four great elements, earth, water, fire and wind; when the four elements each separate, where then is this false body? Seeing through it thus, one will not scheme for this body's many pleasures of enjoyment. Next one must see through the seeing, hearing, sensing and knowing that are present before one: they are entirely the workings of deluded thought, never the true mind. With this deluded mind one creates all kinds of karma; every stirring of mind and moving of thought is nothing but karma, nothing but offense. That single thought is itself the root of the suffering of birth and death. Never follow deluded thoughts along; observe closely in daily life. Wherever a deluded thought arises, see through it at once and extinguish it on the spot. Never let it continue, cling to conditions and go off never to return. If your observation is unsteady and you have nothing to hold on to, simply take the one invocation Amitābha Buddha as your huatou and clutch it tight, never forgetting it thought after thought. With this huatou as your master, whenever a deluded thought arises, raise the Buddha up — this is right mindfulness present before you, and the deluded thought will dissolve of itself without needing to be driven out. In this way, through the twelve double hours, apply the mind closely, with this one thought alone as master and all other deluded thoughts as guests. Once guest and host are distinguished, in time it becomes wholly familiar, and deluded thoughts dissolve of themselves while the true mind reveals itself. If this monk truly has the will, for the great matter of birth and death, let him take this one thought alone as real. All the other worldly tricks — writing poems, practicing calligraphy, and even seeking connections and roaming about in company — are inverted and deluded affairs. If one does not admire true practice but devotes oneself wholly to the superficial and floating, letting the six senses run loose and talking idly without root, wasting the light of day in vain, then not only does one live and die in vain, but one must fear that evil karma is hard to escape, and for a thousand lives and a hundred kalpas there will be no way out.
Instruction to Xu Qingzhi

The Buddha said that all dharmas above and below the three realms are made by the one mind alone. What is above the three realms are the four holy ones who have transcended the world: buddhas, bodhisattvas, śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. What is below the three realms are the ordinary beings of the six paths: gods, humans and asuras, the three good paths; and hell-beings, animals and hungry ghosts, the three evil paths. Thus within the ten dharma-realms, all holy and ordinary beings, all causes and fruits of good and evil, all adornments of body and land, are made by the one mind. And this one mind is none other than the mind that discriminates and knows, present before us in daily life. Since everything is made by the mind and is not produced in stages, it is simply the karma created thought after thought in daily life that turns one about within the ten dharma-realms. If a single thought, born of greed, anger and delusion, commits the ten evils — three of body, four of speech, three of mind — that is the cause of the three evil paths. If a single thought turns the ten evils into the ten good deeds, that is the cause of the wondrous joys of gods and humans. If a single thought forgets both good and evil, so that within one sees no self and without one sees no others, and the mind is still and single, that is the cause of the śrāvaka's escape from suffering. If one contemplates that present pleasure and pain, adversity and compliance, arise and cease by causes and conditions, and that the wheel turns and returns to cessation, that becomes the cause of the pratyekabuddha. If a single thought understands that person and dharmas are without self, that by causes and conditions their nature is empty and there is no doer or receiver, and yet one does not hinder the manifest practice of giving, keeping precepts, patience and the six deeds, converting and saving beings, that is the cause of the bodhisattva. If a single thought suddenly awakens to one's own mind, which from the beginning is bright and vast, excluding nothing, embracing all, saving all, with not one dharma standing before it, and with buddhas and beings equal, that is the cause of buddhahood. Hence this one mind is vast without periphery, from the beginning pure, perfect and luminous. If in daily life one awakens to this thought after thought, then though one dwells amid the dust of toil, one is a person who has transcended the world. This is why Vimalakīrti called it the gate of non-duality. If the layman can embody this and practice it, then all gratitude and resentment, right and wrong, self and others, affliction and the roots of feeling will, with that very thought, be transformed into a treasury of light. In daily life, whatever state appears, try looking at it thus and be mindful of it thought after thought. If you cannot bear it patiently and are obstructed by affliction, the moment you see it arise, raise up the Sixth Patriarch's phrase, From the first not a thing exists, like the vajra king's precious sword; then all afflictions will melt like ice on the spot, and body and mind will become a cool pool. Practice thus with strength; if you can be diligent without retreat, you will at once realize the great ground of liberation. What need is there to seek the Buddhadharma anywhere else?
Instruction to the Chan Monk Ruotan Cheng

The Chan monk Cheng gathered like-minded people at the Eastern Chan Temple of Jinsha and formed the Blue Lotus Society, taking the upholding and recitation of the Lotus Sūtra as their work. Whoever joined the society first had to read the sutra thoroughly and be able to recite it from memory before entering the hall. Within a few years several dozen people could hold it, though they came and went; only this monk remained unwavering in his resolve, and so he made it his lifelong occupation. He asked the old man for instruction, and was told: This sutra is the one by which our teacher, Śākyamuni, the World-Honored One, specially revealed to beings the Buddha's knowledge and vision as the true seed of buddhahood. Hence he recounted his past cause: at the time of Buddha Mahābhijñā-jñānābhibhū he was one of the sixteen princes who heard this sutra and transmitted and upheld it in turn. All who have ever heard it must, life after life, be born together in one place, because they take the holding of this sutra as their practice. Those who were then taught, down to this very life, each received at the assembly on Vulture Peak the prophecy of buddhahood. This plainly shows that this sutra is the true cause and true seed of buddhahood. Therefore it is clearly stated that a Dharma-master who holds the sutra will in this present life obtain purity of the six faculties born of father and mother, exactly as the sutra sets forth; this was proclaimed by the Buddha's own golden mouth, and is no empty word. Since this sutra entered the Middle Kingdom, many have upheld it; yet it was the Great Chan Master Nanyue Huisi alone whose awakening was deep and refined, and the Great Master Zhiyi of Tiantai who, reading and reciting this sutra, beheld the assembly on Vulture Peak still solemnly present and undispersed. Master Si said: This is the Lotus samādhi. None but you can realize it; none but I can recognize it. Therefore Tiantai built upon it the wondrous gate of calming and contemplation and brought forth the purport of the true mark of a hundred realms and a thousand suchnesses. Afterwards, those who relied on calming and contemplation to awaken to the one mind, from Yongjia onward, were not a few. From this it is clear that this sutra is the wondrous practice of buddhahood. Only the Sixth Patriarch said: When the mind is deluded, the Lotus turns the mind; when the mind is awake, the mind turns the Lotus. This too shows the holder of the sutra the gate of supreme meaning. Now, as this monk holds this sutra, let him try, before the scroll is even unrolled, to fling open the true eye on his crown, shatter ignorance, and let the true mark of all dharmas be transparent wherever he touches. Then seeing forms and hearing sounds, he realizes it here and now, and constantly turns such a single scroll of the true sutra, instantly transforming the seeds of love and hate and affliction in the field of the eighth consciousness, accumulated through kalpas, into a treasury of light. To hold it thus is true diligence; this is clearly the true Dharma offered to the Tathāgata. But if one merely takes paper, ink and words as the wondrous Dharma and counts reciting a few lines as holding the sutra, while the mind-ground is not pure and afflictions are not emptied, how is that different from taking a water bubble for a maṇi jewel, or steamed sand for the stuff of rice? Then the ox-hide is not yet pierced through — how could it be merely a screen for the eyes?

For one who studies the Way, an even mind and a vow unto death are the supreme meaning of escaping birth and death; and letting go is the essence of entering the Way. The ancients said: Your aim should be single; if for long you do not retreat, one day you will surely know where the wondrous Way returns. These Five Wuru Peaks are where the old man will return to the real. This monk's mind of taking refuge in the old man has occupied half his life. Now, by good fortune, there is this spot of ground just big enough to plant an awl — precisely the place for you to let go of body and life. Living, we practice together; dying, we return together. You should put down all conditions and make your mind still and single. Here gather two or three like-minded companions. Let the elders devote themselves single-mindedly to recitation of the Buddha's name and earnestly cultivate the pure work, vowing to continue until death. Then the Way of Dharma will long endure and the wisdom-life will not be cut off; thus you will not betray the thought with which you took refuge. Bear in mind that your ancestor Lord Letian had a friendship of three lifetimes with the old man; you should of yourselves take righteousness as your substance and harbor not a second thought. If you keep another thought in reserve, then you are not one who truly lives for birth and death. In ordinary dwelling you must always take the Dharma to heart: uphold the monastery, harmonize the assembly, make inside and outside one body, host and guests one mind, forget both self and others, cut off all right and wrong. Understand that affliction is fundamentally empty — that is the road out of birth and death. This very coolness of mind-ground is the essential gate of the Pure Land. Strive, I urge you, strive!
Instruction to the Chan Monk Ningxutong

The essential of the buddhas' and patriarchs' practice lies only in the two gates of Chan and Pure Land, together with the adornment of the ten thousand practices; this is the right road of practice. Of late, many students inquire into Chan, but misled by the errors of false teachers they are drawn into a thicket of deviant views, fall under the māra of arrogance, and multiply the seeds of outsiders. This is deeply to be feared. Moreover, not one in ten attains liberation. In this way they not only ruin themselves but ruin others — should one not be afraid? For this reason the old man strenuously advocates the true practice of the Pure Land. People of the world do not understand this and all take it lightly as something commonplace, not knowing the wonder of reciting the Buddha's name, and so they make many mistakes. Indeed, reciting the Buddha's name is itself Chan inquiry; there is no second dharma. When reciting, you must first put down all at once every affliction and deluded thought in your breast, every kind of tangled notion of greed, anger, delusion and craving, putting them down until there is nowhere further to put them, and then simply raise up the one invocation Amitābha Buddha, clear and distinct, unbroken in the mind, like a thread strung through beads, or like nocks of arrows fitted one against another with not the least gap between. Leaning on it with such strength, in every place you will not be dragged off and lose it amid conditions and objects. In daily life thus, amid activity you are neither scattered nor confused, and sleeping and waking are as one. Applying the mind so, reciting until at the time of death your mind is single without distraction — this is the moment for transcending birth and death and reaching the Pure Land. But if you merely speak of recitation with the mouth while the mind-ground is impure and deluded thoughts are not removed, and then say that recitation has no efficacy, then even after three lives or sixty kalpas you will have no prospect of getting out. Strive, I urge you.
Reply to the Questions of Prince De

Your Highness has sent an envoy to ask this mountain monk about the direct and speedy gate of practice, saying that Your Highness already keeps the precept of not killing and has eaten vegetarian food for three years, but that you take the final moment as the urgent matter: what dharma should be practiced so as to be at peace at the time of death and not be deluded in the life to come? This shows that Your Highness's habit from past lives has deep roots in prajñā, cultivated over many births; hence now, placed in wealth and honor and a lofty station, you do not obscure the single thought of your original nature, but truly and earnestly inquire into the essentials of the Dharma. This mountain monk is foolish and inferior, yet dares to answer truthfully. The Buddha taught the Dharma to save people as a medicine suited to the illness; the gates of expedient means are many and not of one kind. Since the teaching flowed into this land, those who in every age have relied on and upheld it in practice have had the two gates of Chan and the teachings, followed by everyone alike. In Chan, the patriarchs of the Transmission of the Lamp prized direct awakening to one's own mind. As for the work of application, it is to single-mindedly raise a huatou and inquire, until one clearly sees one's own mind and no further. This is exclusively for people of the very highest faculties, who leap straight in at one bound; and even they need a good teacher to adjust, protect and prod them continually before they gain the right road. In former times there were kings and ministers who could do this, but they were few; it is a practice easier for those who have left home. Now Your Highness dwells in deep seclusion and cannot easily meet good teachers, so I dare not urge this upon you. As for practice according to the teachings, there was formerly Zhiyi of Tiantai, whose Great Calming and Contemplation and Small Calming and Contemplation are essential gates to buddhahood. The Great Calming and Contemplation is verbose and hard to grasp; the Small Calming and Contemplation, though simple and easy, in truth requires that its meaning be understood clearly before one can apply the mind and settle it, and it is not easy to enter. Even if one can understand and perform it, it is hard to make it intimate; in the states of daily life, in adverse and favorable circumstances, it mostly cannot be applied — how much less in the final great matter? This dharma too is not easy for Your Highness to practice, and I dare not recommend it. Now there is only the one gate of the Western Pure Land taught by the Buddha, which takes the single matter of reciting the Buddha's name as essential, visualization of the pure land as the primary practice, recitation of the Mahāyāna sutras as the instigation, the making of vows as the direction, and giving as the adornment of the field of merit. This has truly been followed by all in every age; whether noble or lowly, wise or foolish, all can truly apply effort to it. Therefore, when ten thousand practice, ten thousand have results. I beg Your Highness to give your attention to this. I respectfully set out the daily rules of practice, item by item, as follows.

Our Buddha, to save the suffering beings of the Sahā world, specially taught the gate of the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, taking solely the recitation of Amitābha Buddha and the vow for rebirth as the practice. That land has the Amitābha Sūtra in one scroll as its proof. What is spoken in that sutra is all actual matters of that land and its realm — perfectly clear. The method of practice also has its order, like the daily liturgy of monastics; one need not be bound by a set form, but should take recitation of the Buddha's name as the main thing. Every day, rise early, bow to the Buddha, and recite one scroll of the Amitābha Sūtra, or one scroll of the Diamond Sūtra; then take up the beads and recite the name of Amitābha Buddha, either three or five thousand times or ten thousand times. When finished, dedicate before the Buddha and make the vow for rebirth in that land; the words are in the liturgy. This is the morning service; the evening is the same. Let this be your fixed daily lesson, which must never be omitted. It is even better to teach the palace consorts to practice in the same way. This is what our sage ancestor, the benevolent and filial Holy Mother, practiced and left as a model for the palace, and it is still not abandoned today; this is the constant practice. As for the great matter of the final moment, the work must be even more intimate. Each day, besides the two periods of liturgy, throughout the twelve double hours simply lay the one invocation Amitābha Buddha across your heart, never forgetting it, never dulling it; think of nothing of the world's affairs at all, but take the one phrase of the Buddha as your very root of life, clenching your teeth and resolving never to let it go. Even when eating, rising, resting, walking, standing, sitting or lying down, this one invocation of the Buddha is always present before you. When you meet with states of adversity or favor, of joy or anger, of affliction, and your mind is unsettled, then raise this one invocation and press it, and you will see the affliction extinguished on the spot. For affliction thought after thought is the bitter root of birth and death; now by reciting the Buddha's name you extinguish affliction — this is where the Buddha saves one from the suffering of birth and death. If recitation can dissolve affliction, then it can end birth and death; there is no other dharma. If your recitation can master you in the midst of affliction, then you will master yourself in dreams; if you master yourself in dreams, then you will master yourself amid the suffering of illness; if you master yourself amid the suffering of illness, then at the time of death you will be clear and lucid and will know where you are going. This is not hard to do; it only requires that your one thought for birth and death be keen, and that you simply lean on the one invocation of the Buddha and never go searching elsewhere. In time it becomes wholly familiar, and you will naturally attain great peace and ease, great joy and benefit — by no means comparable to the pleasures of the five desires of the world. I beg Your Highness to attend to this dharma; this is true practice, and apart from this there is nothing more direct and economical. Never listen to deviant views and deviant teachings and be confused by them. Further, if Your Highness wishes to know your destination at the final moment, there is another wondrous method; allow me to speak of it. The method lies within the reciting mind: at all times silently form a visualization. Visualize before you a great lotus flower, of whatever color, blue, yellow, red or white, as large as a cartwheel; visualize the shape of the flower clearly. Then visualize your own body seated within the flower, upon its pedestal, sitting upright and unmoving. Visualize the Buddha sending forth radiance to illumine your body. When making this visualization, whether walking, standing, sitting or lying, and without reckoning the years, months, days or hours, you need only have the visualized state clear, so that with eyes open or closed it is perfectly distinct; even in dreams you will see Amitābha Buddha together with Guanyin and Mahāsthāmaprāpta in the midst of the flower, as plainly as in broad daylight. If this flower-visualization is accomplished, that is the moment of ending birth and death. When the time of death comes, this flower will appear before you; you will see your own body seated within the lotus, and Amitābha, Guanyin and Mahāsthāmaprāpta will come together to receive and guide you. In the space of a single thought you will attain rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss and dwell in the stage of non-retrogression, never again returning to undergo the suffering of birth and death. This is truly the practical result of a lifetime's practice accomplished in one life. This dharma-gate is not something invented by monks; it is a direct gate opened up everywhere in the Buddha's sutras. As it is said: There is only the direct path of practice — simply recite Amitābha Buddha. Apart from this there is no other wondrous dharma. I have heard that Your Highness's mind does not seek long life but only wishes to be clear at the end; apart from this there is no dharma by which to become clear. If you fear illness and wish to learn the regulation of breath and the movement of qi in order to expel sickness, that is not a good method; if the qi is not well moved it may bring on serious illness beyond cure. By no means be confused about this. As for the one practice of reciting the Buddha's name, if you can enter into it intimately, then all the rest need not concern you at all. I beg Your Highness to believe it firmly and truly, and never to doubt.
Further.

On the twenty-seventh day of the first month, the monk Yünzhen, in obedience to Your Highness's command, brought your wise words and asked about certain matters. This mountain monk read them over and over, and it is fully evident that Your Highness is investigating the great matter of birth and death, wishing to understand the root and source of nature and life, and to comprehend the purport of the buddhas' and patriarchs' Chan and teachings. This mountain monk is ignorant and does not presume to speak wildly; I have respectfully consulted the scriptures and set out the questions one by one, answering each clearly as follows. I beg Your Highness to peruse them.

First question: concerning the way of the three vehicles, the origin of nature and life, the doctrines of the teachings and Chan, and Bodhidharma's way — why is it called wordless? Where is effort applied on the mind-ground? What is the ultimate end of human life, and where does one finally come to rest? It is also said: whether a Buddha exists or not, what exactly does that mean? And again: within a single stillness there is no self and no others, like great emptiness — what after all is this? Pray explain in detail, one by one, the words of the upper, middle and lower vehicles, and the buddhas' and patriarchs' thought of saving beings. This is what I wish to hear.

Answer: The cardinal doctrine of the Buddha's teaching takes the one mind alone as its principle. As to this mind, it is originally perfect, luminous and vast, utterly without a speck of dust, pure and without anything. Within it there is from the first no delusion or awakening, no birth or death; saint and ordinary are not established, and beings and buddhas are one substance, without two, without difference. This is precisely what Bodhidharma brought from the West, pointing directly at this originally existing true mind and making it the Chan school. Hence he said to Emperor Wu: Vast and open, there is no holiness. If one can suddenly awaken to this mind, birth and death are forever cut off; it lies only in this person's single thought of sudden awakening, and that is named the Tathāgata of suchness. It does not belong to the ranks of cultivation and realization, nor to the gradual stages of the three vehicles. This Chan school regards it as the path above; what the patriarchs of old transmitted was precisely this mind, taken as the ultimate principle, and this is called Chan. This school does not set up words; it prizes only clarity of mind and seeing of nature. As for the work of advance: at first Bodhidharma taught the Second Patriarch. He asked: What are you doing? The Second Patriarch said: I beg the Master to pacify my mind. Bodhidharma said: Bring me your mind and I will pacify it for you. The Second Patriarch said: Seeking my mind, it is utterly unobtainable. Bodhidharma at once confirmed him, saying: I have pacified your mind for you. This one phrase, the mind is unobtainable, is the pointing of the coming from the West. The Second Patriarch asked again: Is there no expedient means? Bodhidharma said: You have only to let outer conditions cease and the inner mind be without gasping, with a mind like a wall; then you may enter the Way. This is the first work taught for the inquiry into Chan. Bodhidharma's way was this and no more; apart from this mind there is no other dharma. Later, as Chan continued long, students could not awaken suddenly, and so there arose the practice of raising a huatou in Chan inquiry. The huatou may be any one; simply take a koan of the ancients, store it in your breast as your huatou, and bring up doubt. The single word nothing is itself the koan. The very place of doubt is the inquiry. Inquire and inquire, and in time the mind-ground suddenly bursts open, like waking from a great dream, and this is called awakening. Inquiry is itself the application of effort; when one is inquiring rightly, not one thought arises in the mind and there is not a single thing, and so it is said to be without self and without others, like great emptiness. The place of awakening is the final resting place. Once one has awakened to one's own mind, the roots of feeling of kalpas of birth and death are all at once cut off. Since one has awakened to this mind, what is the use of speaking of buddhas and beings? Therefore from then on one may come and go at will within the three realms to save beings, forever cut off from all suffering, no longer detained by birth and death — such a one is called a bodhisattva. This is the final resting place of Chan inquiry, and here nature and life are finished. But if one does not awaken to this mind, one is dragged by the good and evil karma made in one lifetime and turns about in the six paths and the various places of suffering, with no final resting place at all. What is called the bitter sea of birth and death, without an other shore, refers precisely to this.

First: The way of the three vehicles is the gate of expedient devices that the Buddha established according to the faculties of beings in order to save them. The whole great canon of sutras has this meaning. As to the Dharma of the one mind, beings and buddhas are one substance and originally there is no body or mind; it is only because of the first thought of deluded movement that this mind was lost, and so an illusory and false body and mind were formed. The present body of blood and flesh in every person is called the form body; the present perceiving, knowing, thinking and deliberating is deluded thought — what the Heart Sūtra calls the five aggregates. The five aggregates are form, feeling, perception, formations and consciousness. The flesh body is the aggregate of form; the mind is the four aggregates of feeling, perception, formations and consciousness. When body and mind know pain, pleasure and so on, that is feeling. Discriminating, craving and seeking without a break in thought is perception. The uninterrupted continuation of that perception is formations. These three are the mind of perceiving, knowing, thinking and deliberating. The consciousness is the root of life. Before the first delusion it was called simply nature; once the true mind was lost and this illusory body and mind existed, the consciousness linked and sustained this body, and so it was named life. This is the origin of nature and life. When the Buddha first appeared in the world he only taught people to awaken to this mind and nothing more. Because they had been deluded so long and could not awaken, the Buddha established expedients: he first taught people to know that this body is the root of suffering, and that suffering arises from the accumulation of afflictions — greed, anger, delusion and craving. So he required people first to cut off afflictions, and then suffering could be escaped. There were people of middling and lesser faculties who practiced accordingly, cut off afflictions, and indeed escaped the suffering of birth and death; these are called the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, the two vehicles of the lesser and middle. Because they can only save themselves and cannot save others, not knowing the meaning of one substance, they obtain only half; hence they are called the Lesser Vehicle. When there are beings of great mind who can both save themselves and save others, benefiting self and others, widely practicing the six pāramitās — giving, keeping precepts, patience, diligence, meditation and wisdom — with these six practices their minds are vast, and they are called bodhisattvas; hence this is the Great Vehicle, also called the Supreme Vehicle. These two vehicles' dharmas are spoken throughout the whole canon; the point is only to make people awaken to this mind and in the end return to the one mind, which is named the Supreme Vehicle and is called buddhahood — the ultimate principle of the teachings. The methods of practice of the three vehicles are very many and cannot be exhausted in speech; practicing any one dharma will bring one out of the suffering of birth and death. There is not only one way; all kinds of expedients simply aim at awakening to this mind, which is the final resting place. Before awakening to this mind, one is wholly within the sea of birth and death, turning with good and evil: if one does good, one is born among gods or humans; if one creates evil karma and indulges greed, anger, delusion and craving, one falls into the three evil paths and suffers immeasurably. As for the dharmas of the three vehicles: if one practices the middle and lesser vehicles, one remains wholly attached to this body, greedily clinging to enjoyments, and the deluded mind cannot be cut off — hence one cannot succeed. If one of the supreme vehicle practices, though one may give and keep precepts, the remaining four practices cannot be complete, and one still cannot at once escape birth and death. Even cultivating good dharmas and being born in the heavens, when the blessing is exhausted one falls again, like a well-bucket wheel, never reaching a final resting place. If one seeks to awaken clearly to this mind, one may end birth and death; but unfortunately the matters and dharmas before one now are tangled, and one cannot bring oneself to inquire with bitter effort. Even if one inquires, without a true good teacher's guidance one may fear to apply the mind wrongly and fall back into deviant paths. In this way, is not a whole life passed in vain? Though one seeks a final resting place, in the end there is none, because enjoying blessings in heaven does not escape the wheel. Therefore the Buddha established a separate direct expedient: the one gate of reciting the Buddha's name and seeking rebirth in the Pure Land. This is accomplished in one lifetime, and at the time of death there is surely a destination. Now I shall set forth for Your Highness the dharma-gate of recitation and the Pure Land.

First question: why was the gate of the Pure Land established? Because the three vehicles' dharmas that the Buddha established require people to practice, and cannot be accomplished in one lifetime; one may fear falling into the bitter sea of birth and death and find it hard to escape at once. If one can inquire into Chan, one may awaken in one lifetime and escape birth and death; but because deluded thoughts come in profusion and habits are deep, one may be unable to inquire. If one has not clearly awakened to this mind, one cannot escape the wheel. Therefore a separate gate, the Western Pure Land, was established. This does not distinguish upper, middle or lower faculties, nor poverty or wealth, noble or base; whoever is willing to practice according to it may accomplish it in one lifetime. As it is said: There is only the direct path of practice — simply recite Amitābha Buddha; there is no greater cleverness. Why is this so? Because the world in which we now dwell is called Sahā, a place of extreme suffering: the suffering of birth, of old age, of sickness, of death, and even the suffering of not getting what one seeks, of meeting one's enemies, and all kinds of suffering beyond telling. Though one be a prince, a marquis, a general or a minister, with wealth, honor and enjoyment and all kinds of pleasures, all are causes of suffering. Because this extreme suffering is hard to escape, the Western Pure Land is spoken of, named the Land of Ultimate Bliss; because in that land only joys are received, it is called Ultimate Bliss. Because that Buddha-land is utterly without defilement, it is called the Pure Land. There is no woman there, and beings are born by transformation in lotus flowers, and so there is no suffering of birth. Its lifespan is without limit, and so there is no suffering of old age and death. Clothing and food come naturally, and so there is no suffering of not getting what one seeks. All the most excellent people assemble in one place, and so there is no suffering of meeting enemies. That land is adorned with the seven treasures, and so there is no gravel, thorns, filth or impurity; it is pure in every way and wholly unlike this world. What the Amitābha Sūtra says is every word an actual fact. Now for all people who seek rebirth in that land there is no other method: simply recite the Buddha's name with a single mind as the primary practice, dedicate daily, and mentally visualize the lotus and your body seated within it. Then at the time of death you will see Amitābha Buddha send forth light to receive and guide you; you will see a great lotus flower surge up before you and see your own body seated upon the flower; in a single thought you are reborn there. Once born in that land, you will never again fall into the bitter paths of birth and death, and you are called a bodhisattva of the stage of non-retrogression. This then is the fruit of a lifetime's practice and one's destination in the life to come — so very clear. Apart from this, any other talk of what states appear at death is deviant teaching. If one does not recite the Buddha's name, then at the time of death the evil states that follow one's evil karma appear, and regret comes too late. This is the most economical and direct gate of practice, the expedient of receiving and guiding that the Buddha specially established.

First: in cultivating the Pure Land one need not seek to awaken clearly to mind and nature. Take recitation of the Buddha's name and visualization as the primary practice, and further take giving, feeding monks, and cultivating all fields of merit as aids to adorning the Buddha-land. In the reciting mind, though one makes the vow for rebirth, one must know that one has first to cut off the root of birth and death before there can be swift effect. What is the root of birth and death? It is the present clinging to the world's various enjoyments, to beautiful forms, seductive sounds, and flavors for the mouth and body — all are roots of suffering. And all thoughts of anger, wrath and resentment, all clinging, deluded and craving thoughts, and all the dharmas of deviant māras, outsiders and false teachers — for instance, the class of deviant people today who falsely claim such teachings as the Perfect Sudden school of Bodhidharma, or who falsely set up the teachings of Nanyang, Pure Emptiness and Non-Action, and verses such as Returning Home — every one of these was fabricated out of thin air by deviant men of recent times. All such words that delude and confuse the people of the world must be spat out completely. Even the techniques of Quanzhen and of gathering yin and yang, and the doctrines of inner and outer alchemy, are all deviant dharmas and must not be believed. Simply believe firmly in the one gate of reciting the Buddha's name: each day recite two scrolls of the Amitābha Sūtra and recite the Buddha's name a certain number of times, or without counting, only never forgetting the Buddha's name in mind after mind. This very thing is the huatou; it is the root and source of nature and life. There is no need to ask what nature and life are, or what one's original face is, or to talk of the three hun and seven po and the original star — all these are talks that falsely identify and falsely point at this body of blood and flesh, and none of them has any final resting place. If you ask how it is while alive and how it is after death: one who does evil while alive has evil states appear at death; one who recites the Buddha's name and seeks the Pure Land while alive has the Pure Land and the Buddha's state appear at death, thus fulfilling what one sought — that is a good thing. If it does not come from the good mind that one sought, then all is the work of deviant māras; never believe wrongly and ruin a hundred kalpas and a thousand lives. Simply look at the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, where this is clearly stated. As for the saying that all marks are delusive, that is a word within the gate of Chan inquiry: one seeks only the pure true mind, which admits not a single thing, and hence it is said that all marks are delusive. But recitation and the Pure Land are originally accomplished by the mind of visualization; the sutra says: When visualization is clarified, a land is formed. Because in Chan inquiry the cutting off of the deluded mind is the hardest thing, therefore pure visualization is used to replace defiled visualization. The appearing of the lotus is precisely the accomplishment of visualization — how can it be dismissed as a delusive mark? Practices differ, each with its own road; they cannot be judged by one standard. All the answers above have been checked one by one against the sutras and teachings of the buddhas and patriarchs; they are not idle talk. As for Chan inquiry, it takes clarity of mind and seeing of nature as primary. As for the one gate of reciting the Buddha's name and seeking the Pure Land, one need not be clear about mind and nature; one simply recites the Buddha's name. Buddha means awake. If one never forgets the Buddha in thought after thought, then thought after thought one is clearly awake; if one's own mind forgets the Buddha, then one is not awake. If one recites until one can recite in dreams, that is constant awareness undimmed. If this mind is undimmed now, then at the time of death this mind will be undimmed; and the place where this mind is undimmed is the final resting place. Your worthy Highness now has the myriad affairs of state and certainly cannot inquire into Chan; only recitation of the Buddha's name is best. No matter whether at leisure or busy, in movement or stillness, it can be recited everywhere; one has only to be mindful without forgetting. There is no other clever method. Foreknowledge is a matter of spiritual powers and need not be sought; in those days the Buddha did not permit the study of such things. When one becomes a Buddha one naturally has spiritual powers without seeking them. The foreknowledge of ghosts and spirits is not something a person can learn; never think of such matters. If one recites the Buddha's name to the end of life, one will naturally know beforehand the time of one's coming; this too is the ordinary accomplishment of the power of recitation and cannot be forced. The above several items I beg Your worthy Highness to examine in detail and take to heart.
