Question: The ancients who had already received the single transmission and the direct pointing, and who also cultivated the pure work and wished for rebirth — did they do so after awakening, rising in practice according to their vow? Or had they not yet awakened and cultivated the two practices together? If they cultivated both together, they would fall into a thieving mind and a mind of forked roads, and how could their effort become a single piece? If they had already awakened, then every dust mote is the Lotus Treasury and every place is a lotus sprout; in the ten directions there is nowhere that is not so — why take pleasure in the West alone?

Answer: It is said in the teachings that there are three Pure Lands: the Land of Tranquil Light, the Land of Real Reward and Adornment, and the Land of Expedient Transformation with Remainder. As for the buddhas and bodhisattvas, and the patriarchs from of old who received the single transmission and awakened to the mind, all enjoy the Dharma-bliss of their own nature, and not one of them fails to return to the Land of Tranquil Light; this is called the mind-only Pure Land. As for every dust mote and every world being a Pure Land, that is the Land of Real Reward and Adornment of the Lotus Treasury, also manifested by the mind alone. As for seeking rebirth in the Western Pure Land, that is called the Land of Expedient Transformation with Remainder, one land among the dust-mote worlds of the Lotus Treasury. This is for those who wish to seek rebirth. The treatise says: When beings are beginners and fear that their faith will not be established and are minded to retreat, they should know that the Tathāgata has a supreme expedient to gather and protect their faith: by single-mindedly recollecting Amitābha Buddha of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and dedicating the roots of good they cultivate, they obtain rebirth through their vow; and because they always see the Buddha to whom they have gone for refuge, they never retreat. This is for those who practice without having awakened, and it is the meaning of Yongming's saying: If one but sees Amitābha, why worry about not awakening? If one cultivates this practice as well, then as the treatise says: If one contemplates that Buddha's true-suchness dharmakāya and practices diligently, one will in the end attain rebirth and dwell in right concentration. How could this be a thieving mind? It is rather that one has not understood the purport of recitation nor the meaning of the Pure Land. Know therefore that one who has awakened will naturally be reborn without seeking it, while one who has not awakened cannot be reborn by reciting with a thieving mind either.

Question: In Chan inquiry one values the non-arising of a single thought; in recitation one values the succession of pure mindfulness. Now the one gate of inquiring while reciting intends both wondrous awakening and the attainment of rebirth. Yet at present, when reciting, mind and Buddha are distinct, while when inquiring, both are cut off at once; hence the work of inquiry gradually prevails and recitation gradually dwindles. How then can one in future both awaken and be reborn?

Answer: That Chan inquiry values the non-arising of a single thought is so. But to say that recitation values the succession of pure mindfulness — that is merely placing the four-syllable name of the Buddha in the mind and calling it pure mindfulness. You do not realize that the uninterrupted succession of the four-syllable name is called tethered mindfulness, not pure mindfulness; it belongs to people of middling and lesser faculties who devote themselves to reciting the Buddha's name and seeking the West, and is precisely the expedient gate of the Pure Land. Now, the phrase inquiring while reciting, intending wondrous awakening, means taking the one invocation of the Buddha as a huatou to inquire into — what is called the koan of reciting the Buddha and inquiring into Chan. Just as the patriarchs from of old taught people to inquire into huatous such as the cypress tree in the courtyard, three pounds of flax, a dried shit-stick, the dog has no Buddha-nature, put it down, Mount Sumeru — take up any one koan, store it in your breast and quietly inquire, using it to block off the root of the intellect so that deluded thoughts cannot proceed. In time the huatou gains power, and suddenly comes a shout, like a bean popping in cold ashes, and the nest of ignorance and karmic consciousness is pressed and shattered to pieces: this is wondrous awakening. Inquiring while reciting is inquired into in the same way. Simply raise up one invocation of the Buddha and then doubt and examine who it is; gaze deeply and search out from where this Buddha arises and who it is, after all, that recites. Doubt on and on, inquire and inquire again; in time it gains power and suddenly you awaken. This is the koan of examining the recitation of the Buddha truly, and it is from the first no different from inquiring into a huatou. In the end one must inquire to the place where not a single thought arises; that is pure mindfulness. The Calming and Contemplation says: If the mind scatters, one should gather it back and return it to right mindfulness. Right mindfulness is no-thought; no-thought alone is pure mindfulness. It is only when right mindfulness is undimmed that it is called succession — how could the unbroken sound of recitation, voice after voice, be taken as the pure mindfulness of inquiry? Such a person not only does not know Chan inquiry; he does not know recitation either. If inquiry truly reaches the point where pure mindfulness appears before him, then the Pure Land need not be sought outside, for in a single thought he arrives there; the attainment of the highest grade of the highest rebirth is where this practice leads.

Question: As for the principle that the mind itself is Buddha and that one should not seek outside — if one's faith in it is sufficient and one's seeing of it is thorough, should one then simply dissolve karma according to conditions, create no new misfortune, and let things roll on freely, waiting for consciousness to dry up and attain of itself? Or should one further arouse doubt and inquire exhaustively with all one's strength, seeking wondrous awakening?

Answer: To have faith that the mind itself is Buddha is merely empty faith; it must be proven by practice. Without practice and proof, faith alone is of no benefit; how could the mere word faith amount to thorough penetration? The ancients said: First awaken, then cultivate — so after awakening one is just right for practice. The old worthies said: When a student attains a single thought that suddenly accords with his own mind, that is wondrous awakening; yet there still remain in the field of the eighth consciousness the seeds of evil habit from measureless kalpas, called the outflowing consciousness of present karma. After awakening, one takes the principle one has awakened to and, through the twelve double hours, closely and continuously purifies the outflowing consciousness of present karma; this is called cultivation. It is not that there is some further cultivation apart from this awakening. Purifying present karma is dissolving old karma according to conditions; it relies entirely on the power of awakening, and only so can one have the strength to purify evil habits. If one has only empty faith, how will one dissolve evil habits? What is called doubt and inquiry is precisely the work of purifying present karma. Before awakening, one must examine where the outflowing consciousness of habitual karma arises; the sutra says: Sitting quietly in mountain forests, contemplate the flowing of one's own mind. After awakening, wherever an evil habit arises, a single illumination dissolves it, naturally like a flake of snow in a red-hot furnace. Dissolving karma after awakening and the work before awakening differ by a day and a kalpa; they cannot be mentioned in the same breath.

Question: In Chan inquiry there are times when for a while no thoughts arise, and then the huatou cannot be raised up, nor can it be pressed down. When responding to conditions, if one manages and carries it along, the ancients reprove one; if one lets it be, it cannot continue. One is simply stuck between movement and stillness. How should one raise and inquire so as quickly to accord?

Answer: When in Chan inquiry there are times when for a while no thoughts arise, this is not true non-arising; it is merely where the huatou has gained power. This place of power cannot last long; when one meets conditions it is lost, or one is shaken and robbed by states, and naturally movement and stillness become two and arising and ceasing do not stop. If one can truly apply the mind, one should work only at the point before a single thought arises. When in time it becomes wholly familiar, not one thought arises, the original substance appears before one, and the constant light is perfectly clear, unchanging through brightness and darkness, with movement and stillness as one — only then is it beaten into a single piece. When one reaches this and responds to conditions, there is no need to manage or carry it; one naturally accords with the Way in free activity. Would the ancients then reprove one? Is this not truly the meaning of non-arising? The work of Chan inquiry lies only in exerting effort at the point before a single thought arises. Inquiring thus, one will naturally accord quickly. If one takes a lightning-flash samādhi as attainment, one will in the end fall into the nest of consciousness and emotion.

Question: Yongjia said: Who is without thought? Who is without birth? Yunju Qi said: Not cutting off discrimination, not abandoning the marks of mind — this seems to say that after awakening there is still thought and recollection. Again Yongquan said: Not permitted to stray; Yangshan said the Zen ghost does not know; and Shishuang said one thought for ten thousand years — these seem to say that after awakening there is no thought or recollection. Is it that thought exists when responding to conditions but not when apart from conditions? Of these two meanings, existence and non-existence, I beg you to hand down a decision.

Answer: What the ancients awakened to is precisely deluded thought, and deluded thought is precisely what is awakened; from the first there are no two kinds. Deluded people sit inside deluded thought and so look for wondrous awakening, supposing it to be something else. The Laṅkāvatāra says: The saints from of old, transmitting one to another, taught that deluded thought is without nature. How could there be two? It is only that when deluded one uses deluded thought, and when awakened one uses one's own mind. How could deluded thought arise again after awakening?

Question: Yongming said: First one enters through hearing and understanding with faith; afterwards one accords with the selfless. Once one enters the gate of faith, one at once ascends to the patriarch's rank. Now the patriarch's rank is very profound — can one ascend it merely by hearing and understanding? Moreover, Yunmen had already penetrated the dharmakāya, and Dongshan insisted on his fully knowing — that is realization, not understanding. Here, to call the rank of understanding the patriarch's rank must surely have a deep meaning.

Answer: The teachings have the four gates of faith, understanding, practice and realization. Of understanding there is the understanding of awakening and the understanding of knowing. If one enters through hearing with faith, that is a matter on the side of knowing and understanding. But when Lingyun saw the peach blossom, or Xiangyan heard the pebble strike the bamboo, and suddenly penetrated their own minds — that is the understanding of awakening, and once one understands, one penetrates one's own mind at once and spits out the very word understanding. As it is said: Having entered this gate, one does not retain knowing and understanding — and that is called the patriarch's rank. If one hears about matters in another's house and understands them, taking them as one's own, how could one be called a patriarch? As for having penetrated the dharmakāya: if the shadow is not forgotten, one is still fallen into consciousness and emotion and still wholly retains knowing and understanding, and this is why the ancients did not prize it. As for one who has truly awakened — not only is his understanding not called the patriarch's rank; it is as said: At the first arousal of the mind one attains bodhi. How could such a one be ranked with those who know and understand?

Question: The First Patriarch presented the Laṅkāvatāra to seal the mind, and Huangmei had people read the Diamond Sūtra to see their nature; and there was Juzhi with the Cundi mantra and Shoushan with the Lotus — these suggest that Chan inquiry does not obstruct recitation and chanting. Yet Yaoshan did not permit the reading of sutras, and Zhaozhou did not delight in recitation of the Buddha's name; and Gaofeng said: When the huatou is dense and continuous, it is itself one unbroken scroll of sutra. This again suggests that chanting and recitation are forbidden and that the value lies in singly raising the mind-seal. From of old one has taken inquiry into the huatou as primary, while also keeping the Avataṃsaka and recitation as daily lessons. Now I wish to stop the lessons and unify the inquiry, keeping only the power of vow. I do not know whether this is permissible.

Answer: The First Patriarch and Huangmei used the Laṅkāvatāra and the Diamond to seal the mind because the way of Chan had but newly come, and they feared that students would err in applying the mind; hence they used the sutras to seal and correct the mind so that it should not go astray. It was not that they took the sutras as their own understanding. Juzhi's Cundi was the taking of a mantra as a huatou for inquiry, a case of entering by conditions. As for Shoushan and the Lotus, that was after awakening, done at leisure as a Buddhist work; it is what is called, when the mind is awake, the mind turns the Lotus — not the making of recitation into a meritorious practice. Those who did not permit the reading of sutras or recitation of the Buddha's name feared precisely that students would lose themselves and take these as literal dharmas. When a Chan student has not yet awakened, there is no harm in chanting and recitation; one borrows the empowerment of the Dharma's power as an aid to practice, as in the three-period repentance, which the ancients could not do without. After awakening, reciting sutras lets the light of the mind shine through every word, and all becomes wondrous practice. How could that be compared to tracing the lines and counting the ink, like a spring bird crying by day?

Question: Do not worry that you will not become a Buddha; worry only that the Buddha will not understand you — this is an old maxim. Students today do not devote themselves to true practice but to sharp repartee and turning words; that is a fault. Yet if one knows one has not awakened and constantly prods oneself, it is only because one's insight is not yet clear and one fears one is practicing blindly and smelting in the dark; hence one engages in question and answer, exchange and response, with teachers and fellow students. Is this also harmless? But if one's study cannot bear discussion, and one must wait until after awakening to utter a word, then one's insight is still deficient — from whom shall practice begin? Moreover, refining principle and nature, and deciding right from wrong, as in three ascents and nine climbs, or one phrase spanning a thousand mountains — are these not all before awakening?

Answer: In ancient times those who had awakened to the mind were called clear-eyed people. When adepts met, it was like two mirrors reflecting each other: whether words were spoken or not, the Way was present at a glance; they did not insist on exchanging repartee and taking cleverness as the measure of height. Students of later times, wild and arrogant, run about with glib tongues, and are truly not worth taking. But if a student has doubts and, before a clear-eyed person, sincerely asks for instruction and lays bare his own mind, that too is not a meeting of tongues. As for widely consulting teachers, it is only to decide about this mind; what harm is there in lingering in the weeds and discussing things plainly? That is the true man of the Way. To busy oneself with repartee and social exchange is the business of the door-frame and threshold, not the real thing. One who truly inquires and truly awakens will never fall into this.

Question: One who sees his own nature gains freedom within birth and death; one who is master of himself can transform karma at the point of death. Of the patriarchs who gained such freedom, let us not speak; but as for Master Caotang Qingyin and others of that kind, how is it that they were deluded as soon as they passed to another life? Is it that awakening has its depths and shallows and habit its lightness and weight? Or is it that, out of intensified great compassion, their root was high but their traces were low, and people simply did not know it? If not, how can students put their trust in the gate of seeing one's nature?

Answer: What the ancients meant by saying that one awakening ends birth and death is that one awakens to the dharmakāya of one's own nature. There still remain beginningless ignorance and the seeds of habit accumulated through kalpas, all of them bitter causes of birth and death, which are not exhausted at once; hence one must practice for many kalpas before accomplishing the buddha-way. For example, a bodhisattva of the seventh faith has already awakened to his own nature and entered the stage of non-retrogression, yet he passes through forty-two further stages and gradually cuts off the habit of ignorance before accomplishing the buddha-way. How could the awakening of the seventh faith be taken as the final ending of birth and death? Know therefore that transformation birth-and-death still corresponds to subtle suffering; hence it is said that bodhisattvas have the dimness of passing through a womb. What is called transforming karma means only that the power of the Way is surpassing, and so one can transform it; it does not mean that fixed karma is necessarily dissolved. In truth, awakening has its depths and shallows and habit its thickness and thinness. But after awakening, one dwells in birth and death without being detained by them, coming and going freely; hence it is called transformation birth-and-death. One who has awakened to the mind, even if deluded within birth and death, awakens easily and will never fall into great inversion. The sutra says: Once it becomes the substance of true gold, it is never again ore. How could one beforehand worry that he will be deluded again, and so slight the gate of seeing one's nature? As for the case of a high root with low traces, that is not discussed here. Yet even the Buddha could not escape fixed karma, and that too is not the fault of awakening to the mind.
Reply to Duan Huanran, Remonstrance Official

Question: The perfect and wondrous true mind is never obstructed except by the five aggregates, and entry into the Tathāgata's ground is never accomplished except by breaking through the aggregates. The Śūraṅgama's fifty-five stages set out the arrangement in detail: from shallow to deep, one must break through a certain aggregate and only then mount a certain stage. Yet the matching of the obstructions to be broken with the stages has not yet been made clear by the various commentators. Can it be that the learning is too hard to conceive and the weighing too hard to reach, and so they set it aside? The sutra says: One who has exhausted the aggregate of feeling, though not yet free of outflows, has a mind that leaves its body; from that ordinary body he passes through the sixty holy stages of the bodhisattva. From this it is evident that the breaking of the aggregate of form is certainly within the three gradual stages, beyond doubt. Moreover, the practice of true cultivation and the advance through the various merits all arise from the body of form; the breaking of the form aggregate can be verified point by point. Yet the aggregates of feeling and perception and the rest, drawn into the sixty stages, are still not decisively distinguished. And the sutra says further: When the consciousness aggregate is exhausted, it is like pure crystal containing the precious moon; thus one transcends the ten faiths and so on. From this it is evident that the five aggregates should be included in the arrangement; it is only that later people were not careful. If a certain aggregate is not exhausted, one cannot transcend the ten faiths; if a certain aggregate is not exhausted, one cannot transcend the ten dwellings, and so on. Only when the consciousness aggregate dissolves does one transcend the sixty stages. Now if you say that breaking the aggregates is one thing and need not be merged with the sixty stages, and the stages are another thing and need not be merged with the breaking of the aggregates, then there are two separate approaches. Moreover, if the successive stages are not merged with the five aggregates, then within the arrangement the merit of vanquishing māras is lacking and the arrangement fails to be an arrangement. If the breaking of the aggregates is not merged with the three worthies and ten sages, then within the breaking of the aggregates the stages of cultivation and realization are missing and the breaking fails to be a breaking. I beg the Master to analyse it point by point and open up my clinging delusion. Today those who plunder the records and copy the cases value only clear eyes and not practical conduct, saying, Walking on the crown of Vairocana, what five aggregates are there? What arrangement? Great false speech is thereby accomplished — how extreme will the harm be? Even the patriarchs of the Chan school who attained the Way say that once all is understood, all is finished, and that one need not pass through three asaṃkhyeya kalpas. Now, leaving aside the spiritual powers of the ten grounds, even a bodhisattva abiding in the resolve of vow can roam the ten directions, going wherever he wishes — did the eminent worthies of the Transmission of the Lamp have such means? At the first arousal of the mind one at once attains perfect enlightenment; I fear this is only to be classed among the first dry wisdom, and is not necessarily the final mind of vajra dry wisdom. Next, I have seen Gushan's commentary on the passage about the exhaustion of the consciousness aggregate and the mutual use of the faculties: it is precisely the round teaching's stage of similarity, where within the seventh faith the delusions of thought are already exhausted; and one who can enter vajra dry wisdom passes from the stage of similarity beyond into the final mind of Equal Enlightenment. Tiantai, expounding the round teaching, says that a person of sharp faculties may in one lifetime leap up to the ten grounds, which accords with this. On first reading that text I could not help clapping my hands and saying: If the consciousness aggregate is exhausted, thus one transcends the ten faiths, ten dwellings, ten dedications, ten grounds, Equal Enlightenment, and so on. The word transcend again means not passing through the fifty-five stages. If so, then after the three gradual stages the five aggregates are at once broken; and if the aggregates are broken, can all fifty-five stages be transcended at once? If so, then apart from the arrangement there is another separate approach. I beg the Master to tell me in detail. Like a farmer parched for rain, I count each day as a year. This request for instruction is more earnest and deeper than before. I pray you do not begrudge your gold and jade. Duan Ran of Wuchang bows his head.

Answer: From your question about the depths and shallows of breaking the aggregates in the Śūraṅgama, and their sameness or difference from the fifty-five stages, I see that this is a state personally realized by the buddhas and bodhisattvas dwelling in their own samādhi, and not something ordinary sentiments may presume to measure. The teachers of former times never even raised this doubt; even the Record of the Mirror of the Source, which plumbs the very source of nature and characteristics, does not discuss it, and students have never given it any attention. Even my own General Discussion only ventures a little on the three gradual stages and the concluding passage on stages, and does not correlate them in detail. Your question shows deep insight. This rustic is shallow and dim, and moreover his meditation is not deep and the five aggregates are not broken; how should I dare speak wildly about states within samādhi? But because the layman's mind for the Dharma is keen and his questioning earnest, I dare, relying on the measure of the holy word, to set out its general outline. What are called the five aggregates are the instruments by which all beings universally undergo the suffering of birth and death. No practitioner of the Way has ever transcended birth and death without breaking the five aggregates. Hence the Tathāgata's appearance in the world was solely to break beings' five aggregates, the instruments of birth and death; the whole teaching of one age is entirely talk of breaking the aggregates, scattered through the five periods and spoken everywhere, only without sequence. The Śūraṅgama alone gathers in the whole teaching of one age, embracing delusion and awakening, cultivation and realization, cause and fruit, and exhausts both the holy and the ordinary paths, so that practitioners may have it as the single road to nirvāṇa; therefore its stages of cultivation and realization are detailed from beginning to end. Moreover, it specially sets forth the states of breaking the aggregates within samādhi because the true cultivation in this sutra enters deeply through the single gate of meditation and tests its depth by the breaking of the aggregates. Hence its stages differ from those given in the Avataṃsaka and the Necklace Sutra. In the Avataṃsaka's perfect and round ocean of fruition, one stage contains all stages; though an arrangement is set out, it does not speak of cutting off and realizing, its point being to reveal the perfectly fused. Hence at the first arousal of the mind one at once attains perfect enlightenment, taking the fruit of enlightenment as the causal mind. The Necklace Sutra's stages, though detailed, intend cutting off and realizing in parts, and so define the arrangement by the delusions of view and thought, of dust and sand, and of ignorance, as Tiantai sets forth. This sutra is utterly different from those two: it rests solely on the Śūraṅgama's great samādhi, sudden awakening and gradual cultivation, and so takes the mind of non-arising and non-ceasing as the ground of practice — that is, one first awakens to the wondrous perfect true mind as the ground of the arousal of the mind, and with this mind gradually cuts off habit, using that to determine the depth of the stages. This is exactly the Awakening of Faith, where the arousal of the mind and practice take awakening to true suchness as the ground; but as to cutting off delusion, that treatise relies largely on the characteristics school's cutting off and realizing, and specifically defines the stages by the six coarse and three subtle marks — which is called first awakening, then cultivation. Hence in the treatise it is easy to understand the stages as defined by breaking delusion, while in this sutra it is hard to reconcile the stages as defined by breaking the aggregates. Why? According to the treatise, the stage of faith cuts off the three coarse delusions of grasping, of conceptualizing names, and of producing karma; the three worthies cut off continuity and the mark of intellect, two delusions that are the subtle within the coarse and the coarse within the subtle; from the first ground to the seventh ground one cuts off the mark of manifestation among the three subtle; from the eighth ground to Equal Enlightenment one cuts off the mark of turning; and at the vajra stage one finally cuts off the mark of karma. This is the treatise's clear statement of cutting off and realizing. Now if one matches the five aggregates against the delusions and aligns them with the height of the stages, the sutra's meaning is quite otherwise. For the sutra has clear words: In principle one must awaken suddenly, and with the awakening they are all dissolved — this is not to pass through the stages. In fact they must be removed gradually, and exhausted successively according to stage — this again defines the stages by cutting off. That this sutra is first awakening and then cultivation exactly accords with the treatise's meaning. But according to the treatise, delusion and karma are cut off first, in the three worthies, and ignorance afterwards, on entering the grounds, which differs somewhat from this sutra. Examine the sutra's text: within the three gradual stages one already obtains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas, and from there gradually cultivates and establishes the holy stages. Now the patience of non-arising is obtained only when one has entered the grounds and realized equal true suchness; so the sutra's intent is that within the three gradual stages one takes true suchness alone as the ground of practice. And it says: The reversed stream becomes wholly one; the six functions do not operate; the lands of the ten directions are luminously pure, like crystal with the precious moon suspended within. And the later passage says: If the consciousness aggregate is exhausted, it is like pure crystal containing the precious moon; thus one transcends the ten faiths and on to the perfect brightness of Equal Enlightenment, entering the Tathāgata's wondrous ocean of adornment. By this buddha-word it is proved that within the three gradual stages one has already transcended the stages, and that before mounting the stages one has already broken the consciousness aggregate, without waiting for the stage of similarity and faith. How then should I presume to match the sequence of breaking the aggregates to the stages? Examining the Buddha's intent carefully, it must not be so. The true meaning of this sutra, in which it greatly differs from the other sutras, is that those sutras, according to time and faculties, speak of a single segment of cultivation and realization, and the delusions they break are likewise weighted according to faculties — they are medicines suited to an illness for a time. This sutra gathers in the whole teaching of one age, excluding no faculty, and lays its weight on singly breaking the root of birth and death, pointing specifically to the habit of lust as the root of birth and death, with the great samādhi as the weapon that breaks the enemy. Hence the sutra specially brings out the two kinds of ignorance, that which produces karma and that which moistens rebirth; the great samādhi directly breaks the fundamental ignorance of the eighth consciousness, and by the samādhi one hews to the end. Even if the eighth consciousness is not broken, the coarse delusions of view, thought and dust-and-sand fall away of themselves. As for taking the mind of non-arising and non-ceasing as the ground of practice, this is precisely taking the vajra mind as the ground of meditation. Hence the sutra says: This is named the wondrous lotus, the vajra king, the precious enlightenment. From this we see that when one first cultivates samādhi, within the three gradual stages, hewing with samādhi, one has already broken the eighth consciousness and penetrated the vajra mind-ground — precisely, in principle one must awaken suddenly, and with the awakening they are all dissolved — and so one can transcend the stages. If one says that from there one establishes the holy stages, then that is: in fact they must be removed gradually, and exhausted successively according to stage — which means, by gradual cutting off of the habit of ignorance through kalpas, and specifically according to thickness and lightness, to judge the depth and height of the stages. Thus, in terms of sudden awakening and gradual cultivation, entering the stages by breaking the aggregates is from the first not two roads. This meaning accords exactly with Weishan's saying: If a person in a single thought suddenly penetrates his own mind, this is called awakening; and then with what he has awakened he purifies the outflowing consciousness of present karma, and this is called cultivation; there is no other cultivation apart from this. Beings follow the stream of birth and death, and the stream is of four kinds: the stream of desire, the stream of existence, the stream of views, and the stream of ignorance. Now in the three gradual stages, desire and craving dry up, faculties and objects no longer pair, and the remaining substance before one is not renewed in birth: this is the cutting off of the three streams of desire, existence and views. It is named the stage of dry wisdom because there is a dry wisdom not yet linked with the Tathāgata's stream of Dharma-water — that is, the stream of ignorance is not yet dried. This stream of ignorance is the stream of ignorance within the vajra mind, which the Chan school calls the outflow of true permanence. Hence the sutra's concluding passage on stages says: This awakening first attains the initial stage of dry wisdom within the vajra mind. This means that from the earlier gradual stages, having obtained dry wisdom, up to Equal Enlightenment, only then is the stream of the habit of ignorance within the vajra mind dried up. From this we see that within the three gradual stages the eighth consciousness is already broken and one suddenly awakens to one's own mind; from entering faith onward up to Equal Enlightenment one cuts off the habit of ignorance throughout — precisely, in fact they must be removed gradually, and exhausted successively according to stage. The reason ignorance must be exhausted only after passing through the stages is that from the realm of true purity a single thought of ignorance suddenly arose and so birth and death began; through measureless kalpas, giving rise to delusion and creating karma, all has been the fault of ignorant deluded thought. Because the duration of birth and death through vast kalpas is long, and one is dyed with craving and the habit is deep, one must use the vajra mind to polish and smelt again and again before one can return to the original mind-ground. Hence from the stage of faith onward it is said that the perfect wonder opens and unfolds and the middle way is pure and true, and at the end it says, thus layer upon layer, single and repeated, twelve — which precisely reveals the work of this great samādhi in wearing away habit. Again the sutra says that each of the five aggregates has deluded thought as its root. If breaking the aggregates were matched to the stages, then in the sutra's very first passage on faith it says: With this mind flowing in within the middle, all deluded thoughts are extinguished without remainder. How then could one carry the aggregates into the stages? If one practices while carrying deluded thought, it is not called true cultivation. Moreover, in the three gradual stages desire and craving dry up, faculties and objects no longer pair, and the remaining substance is not renewed in birth: this is already to have left the birth and death of the three realms. The later passage says that when the consciousness aggregate is exhausted one transcends the turbidity of life — how could it be merely the breaking of the form aggregate? Feeling is appropriation: the four elements have pain, pleasure and so on. If the feeling aggregate is not broken one cannot attain right feeling; if the perception aggregate is not broken it is hard to enter the wondrous śamatha; if the formations aggregate is not broken, arising and ceasing do not stop and it is not right concentration; if the consciousness aggregate is not broken, one has not awakened to the true mind and it is hard to establish the stages. By this it is proved that within the three gradual stages the five aggregates are already broken, and that one certainly does not carry the five aggregates into the stages. How could it be merely the breaking of the form aggregate? Only when all five aggregates are broken is it called true awakening; only when one advances by breaking the eighth consciousness is it called true cultivation. Thus the breaking of the five aggregates is the sudden awakening to the principle, and the stages thereafter merely concern the great samādhi wearing away the habit of ignorance accumulated through kalpas — precisely, in fact they must be removed gradually. As for the fifty-five stages and their wondrous virtues: because the tathāgatagarbha contains Ganges-sands virtues that accord with nature, which had been turned by ignorance into Ganges-sands habits of birth and death, now by the vajra illusory samādhi one polishes those habits and transforms them into spiritual powers and wondrous function. Because what is transformed is shallow, the stage is low; because what is transformed is deep, the stage is high. Guifeng said: Awakening to the fault of the former former is named the latter latter stage. Seen thus, the great meaning of this sutra is that one single-mindedly investigates the mind, advances to break ignorance, and defines the stages to show the depth of realization — not comparable to cutting off and realizing in parts. That one first breaks the aggregates and afterwards enters the eight stages clearly shows that it is not a matter of matching the breaking of the five aggregates to the stages. How could one insist that breaking the aggregates runs parallel with the arranged stages? As for the teaching on breaking the aggregates, the Buddha, fearing that practitioners would be content with a little and would practice in confusion, specially set it forth to guard against error; it is not that he used it to explain the stages. Moreover, that one who has not broken the consciousness aggregate falls into the two vehicles can be known. If one in the Chan gate suddenly awakens to one's own mind and suddenly leaves birth and death, one does not fall into ranks — that is, within the three gradual stages one suddenly breaks the eighth consciousness and naturally transcends the stages. Yet though the patriarchs speak of transcending, they speak only of the plain dharmakāya Buddha, who does not necessarily possess the adornment of marks and radiance, spiritual powers and wondrous function. Even the buddhas and tathāgatas: none became a Buddha without awakening to his own mind. If one awakening finished everything, why should the buddhas have had to pass through three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas? People today, before their cushion is steady, use worldly cleverness to plunder the koans of the ancients, flaunt their own knowledge and views, and falsely claim to have realized sagehood, thinking themselves to surpass buddhas and patriarchs. Such are arrogant and conceited persons who claim to have attained what they have not and fall into great false speech — should one not fear it? How could such people be mentioned in the same day as true practitioners, whether they break the aggregates or not? Yesterday, traveling east, I saw many Chan practitioners, and not a few had fallen into such conceit. This rustic specially brought up the breaking of the aggregates to seal and correct them, and those who heard were ashamed and submitted, and their deviant views were considerably broken. I have seen laypeople discussing Chan fall into this sickness often. For true cultivation today, one should take as the urgent task the practice of the three gradual stages, the sudden awakening to one's own mind, and the sudden transcendence of birth and death. If one's own mind is once clear, the consciousness aggregate breaks of itself, and the four earlier aggregates break of themselves without needing to be broken. It is like bringing one's head to the white blade — like cutting the spring wind: how could the form aggregate obstruct it? Again it is said: The old monk can turn the twelve hours; and again: The in-breath does not dwell in the realm of aggregates, the out-breath does not touch any condition — how could he be within the feeling, perception and formations aggregates? The Sixth Patriarch knew his destination at death — was that not going wherever his vow wished? Such a one is hardly to be compared with those who falsely claim to have realized sagehood. We should prize only the clear investigation of our own mind and the single matter of escaping birth and death, and need not debate whether the breaking of the aggregates accords with the stages. Weighing it by principle and proving it by the holy words, such is my dim and inferior view; let the learned instruct me.
Guangzhi of the West Hall Asks About Six Doubts Concerning the Teaching Vehicle

First question: The ancients, in classifying the teachings, said that the two forms were both projected and the two beginnings were simultaneous; that the Buddha first taught the Avataṃsaka, intended for the Great Vehicle, with the two vehicles wholly excluded; and that when he turned the wheel of the Four Noble Truths at Deer Park, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana had not yet abandoned their deviant teachers and left home. Why then in the concluding passage of the Avataṃsaka are there śrāvakas such as Śāriputra? If we go by the concluding text, the two vehicles did hear the Avataṃsaka; why then is it asserted that the two vehicles were wholly excluded? Text and meaning contradict each other. I beg you to distinguish and explain.

Answer: The teachings say that the buddhas of the ten directions have one body and one wisdom; therefore in the buddha-lands of the ten directions only the One Vehicle Dharma is taught. Hence at the site of bodhi, immediately upon attaining perfect enlightenment, he taught the Avataṃsaka as the Supreme One Vehicle Dharma, intended solely for beings of great faculties; this is called teaching according to real wisdom. But since beings' faculties are not uniform, those of middling and inferior understanding neither see nor hear it, and so are wholly excluded. Therefore, in response to inferior faculties, he manifested a small transformation body, accomplished the Way through the eight phases, and at Deer Park taught the three vehicles' dharmas. It is said that the Buddha's true dharmakāya is like empty space, appearing in form in response to things like the moon in water; because he merely responds to faculties, he manifests a body, and what he teaches is expedient wisdom. At the Avataṃsaka assembly, in the Jetavana Grove, when Mañjuśrī, king of elephants, turned about, Śāriputra and six thousand bhikṣus attained the Way at his words; these too were bodhisattvas of the grounds, named great arhats. Now since the Buddha manifested a small response body and showed himself born among humans, and the various outsiders clung firmly to their view of self and were not easily gathered and converted, Śāriputra and the others likewise appeared as śrāvakas to assist and spread the conversion of the Dharma, becoming an echoing assembly — the sort who are inwardly hidden and outwardly manifest, not real śrāvakas. The assertion that the two vehicles were wholly excluded refers to real śrāvakas who cling to marks; and the reproof that Śāriputra and the others received was precisely to strike the drum of the Dharma's conversion. It is much like a stage play, where each takes a part to stir up feelings of sorrow, joy, parting and reunion, and when the play breaks up there is no involvement at all. So the bodhisattva's benefiting of beings is like play: responding when tuned, meeting by chance — how could it be a literal dharma?

Second question: In the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Universal Eye did not see Samantabhadra. Three times he entered samādhi and surveyed the three thousand great thousand worlds without seeing him, and then came and told the Buddha. The Buddha taught him that in the samādhi of stillness, if he raised a thought he would see him. Universal Eye had but to raise one thought and at once saw him in empty space. If Samantabhadra's body is the one true dharma-realm, he should be seen within samādhi — why was he not seen? If Samantabhadra is a body of form and marks, he should have been seen before entering samādhi — why did the Buddha teach that he was seen only when a thought was raised?

Answer: The dharmakāya is without marks; even Universal Eye could not gaze upon it. That he sought it in samādhi and did not see it is because the dharmakāya has no mutual seeing of this and that. Know therefore that what can be seen belongs to the second approach; hence it was seen only when a thought was raised.

Third question: In the Awakening of Faith, true suchness perfumes from within, and so there is deluded mind; wearied of the suffering of birth and death, one seeks nirvāṇa. The deluded mind is of two kinds: first, ordinary beings and the two vehicles perfume and cultivate relying on the consciousness of things; second, bodhisattvas perfume and cultivate relying on the karmic consciousness. Students today inquire relying only on the consciousness of things and cannot rely on the karmic consciousness. Chan inquiry is originally a Great Vehicle gate; if one inquires relying on the consciousness of things, it becomes instead the practice of ordinary beings and the two vehicles. And if in inquiry one uses both consciousnesses at once, that contradicts the ancients' saying: Inquire apart from mind, intellect and consciousness. I beg you to open and decide this.

Answer: The teaching that ordinary beings and the two vehicles cultivate relying on the consciousness of things and that bodhisattvas cultivate relying on the karmic consciousness refers to arousing the mind and attaining realization in dependence on consciousness. Now when a Chan student arouses the mind, though it be the consciousness of things, his resolve aims directly at smashing the lacquer bucket of the karmic consciousness and penetrating straight to the one point above, before delusion began, not falling into the nest of the two consciousnesses. If he is content with a little, then he cannot be free of mind, intellect and consciousness.

Fourth question: The ancients said: I do not prize your conduct, only your insight. And again: If insight is not clear, one falls into a pit. Nowadays explanations in various quarters are of two kinds. One says that broad learning in sutras and treatises, with understanding based on them, is called insight. Another says that only after awakening clearly is there insight. If learned understanding is insight, why does the Chan school not permit the reading of the teachings? If insight comes only after awakening, then what dharma should a beginner take as insight in his practice, so as to avoid the calamity of falling into a pit?

Answer: Understanding as insight is of three kinds: there is understanding by learning, understanding by faith, and understanding by awakening. If one understands from the teachings or from the patriarchs' koans the ultimate point of the buddhas and patriarchs, not falling into side branches, this, though it is named insight, is understanding based on a ground. If one has not personally met with the spoken teachings but simply resolves with certainty to believe in one's own mind, in which there is not a single thing, that is understanding by faith. If through inquiry one one day clarifies what is originally possessed, that is understanding by awakening. All three are named insight. But understanding based on another mostly falls into the obstruction of knowledge and views. Understanding by faith, even so, still requires practice to reach true realization. Understanding by awakening, though it be a single thought of sudden awakening, still has beginningless subtle obstructions of delusion which must also be purified. Though these three kinds of insight are prized, without conduct one can in the end hardly reach the ultimate. The insight prized by the ancients was based on faculties; it is not that conduct is not valued. The occasional words of the ancients must not be taken as literal dharmas.

Fifth question: The ancients said that inquiry should be carried on while carrying firewood and drawing water and while traveling on foot. Students today hold that one should sit quietly, for then the work of inquiry has power; but in the four dignified postures, when in contact with things, thoughts fly in confusion and the huatou sinks away. If one only sits quietly, that again contradicts the ancients' conduct; if one engages with things, the mind is scattered all day. How can a student be made to be without conflict between movement and stillness in daily life?

Answer: When the ancients did their work, they wanted it observed in walking, standing, sitting and lying, in the four dignified postures; they did not teach you to sit rigidly like a dead thing. Because one who first enters Chan has a mind much scattered and stirred, one provisionally takes to quiet sitting to gather the mind; but in truth one must take what is done in stillness and test it in the midst of movement, to see how it fares. If the mind is applied closely and continuously, movement and stillness are naturally as one and are beaten into a single piece. That thoughts now fly in confusion before objects means that the huatou has no power at all — can such a one be a true practitioner? What matters now is only that the huatou gain power; then, regardless of movement or stillness, one will naturally not be turned about by them.

Sixth question: The sutra says that mind, Buddha and beings — these three are without difference. It also says that the realm of the buddhas is equal and the realm of beings is equal. It also says that only when all beings are saved does one accomplish the buddha-way. If beings and buddhas are equal, then the Buddha has no meaning of saving beings; how is it that only when all beings are saved does one accomplish the buddha-way? And if the buddhas and bodhisattvas save all beings, the realm of the buddhas would seem gradually to increase and the realm of beings gradually to decrease. How then can beings and buddhas be called equal?

Answer: Mind, Buddha and beings are from the beginning equal. Because beings are the beings within the Buddha's mind, the Buddha saves the beings of his own mind. If the mark of beings is empty, that is the saving of all beings, and one accomplishes the Buddha of one's own mind. Even if one mind were wholly made into beings, that would be beings making themselves into the beings of their own minds, and the realm of the buddhas would not decrease. Even if the realm of beings were exhausted, it would only be the dissolving of each one's own realm of beings; because the mind is equal, the Buddha does not increase either. The Buddha sees the realm of beings as empty; but if beings' own minds are not empty, then beings do not decrease either. It is like the vast sky when clouds gather and mist darkens it: the sky does not decrease; when the clouds scatter and the mist clears, the sky does not increase. Though it be darkened all day and cleared all day, the substance of the sky remains limpid. How then could there be increase or decrease in the realm of the buddhas?
Reply to Dajie's Six Questions

First question, on keeping the precepts: A beginner does not know how to keep the precepts and fears that every movement is a fault; receiving them has its order, and one must certainly not be reckless. Yet within them the great and small vehicles are distinguished and the expedient and the real have their applications; though faculties differ in sharpness and dullness and capacities vary in depth, there are inevitably abuses. I beg you to set out the rules of conduct, so that the sharp may look up and follow them and the dull may broaden their scope.

Answer: The precepts established by the Buddha are recorded in detail in the Vinaya. His original intent was that because beings have eighty-four thousand afflictions, he set up eighty-four thousand rules of discipline as medicines matched to the illness, wishing to cure the illness of affliction and make the dharmakāya pure. Because faculties are great or small, the precepts have three grades: the ten precepts of the śrāmaṇera, the two hundred and fifty precepts of the bhikṣu, and the bodhisattva's ten major and forty-eight minor precepts. The two kinds of precepts, those of the śrāmaṇera and the bhikṣu, were established according to circumstances and are called preventive precepts, meaning that they block and stop transgressions. Though great and small alike observe them, they belong mostly to the Lesser Vehicle: one merely restrains the body from acting. One who can restrain the mind from arising is of the Great Vehicle, yet this too remains within the precepts of marks and affairs. As for the ten major and forty-eight minor precepts spoken of in the Brahmā Net Sūtra, they are called the precepts of nature; they were spoken by my original teacher, the reward-body Buddha Rocana, as the mind-ground gate of all buddhas, named the Vajra Jewel Precepts, and he commanded Śākyamuni to transmit and spread them in turn. What is meant by the precepts of nature is this: to understand and penetrate that one's own nature is pure and from the beginning undefiled, and to awaken suddenly to the originally existing pure dharmakāya, whose nature is inherently complete — this is called the precepts. The sutra says: If a person receives the Buddha's precepts, he at once enters the rank of the buddhas. Hence all that Śākyamuni taught in forty-nine years was but the transmission of this precept-dharma; and what he showed at the end by holding up the flower was but the showing of this nature of the precepts. What the patriarchs of every generation awakened to was but the perfecting of this light of the precepts. Therefore, when one contemplates all beings, the seed of buddha-nature is from the beginning equal, because all alike possess the equal dharmakāya. If one contemplates beings by way of buddha-nature, then whenever a single thought of killing, stealing, lust or lying arises, or one speaks of the faults of the four assemblies, praises oneself and disparages others, or slanders the Three Jewels, one cuts off the Buddha's wisdom-life, no different from killing a Buddha; hence the ten major items are set out. If one contemplates beings by way of the equal dharmakāya, then there is nothing to kill, steal from, lust after or lie about, nor anyone to disparage, for these are the perfect and sudden precepts. What they chiefly value is the seed of buddha-nature alone, which is the Buddha's wisdom-life. Not only those of sharp faculties can receive them; even paṇḍakas and the two-sexed, men given to lust and women given to lust, and even ghosts and spirits — anyone who understands the master's words is fit to receive them. One need only believe that the seed of buddha-nature in all beings is the equal dharmakāya. If one can contemplate thus, then in every state encountered in daily life one is wholly within the ground of the light of the precepts. Then not only does one not restrain the body from acting; in killing, stealing, lust and lying, with every glance and every thought the buddha-nature appears before one and is instantly transformed into a mass of light. How could it be merely that the mind does not arise? Yet as to the way of keeping them: with the preventive precepts it is indeed hard, for it lies wholly in restraining the three karmas and subduing transgressions. But the precepts of nature are truly hard: one must hold them with a single mind of vajra and not lose them. A single thought of dullness, and the whole body falls — is this a small matter? Hence the Avataṃsaka, for those at the beginning of the ten faiths who keep these precepts, sets out the Chapter on Pure Conduct with its one hundred and twenty great vows, so that in daily life there is no place of leakage; yet this still follows marks and affairs. As for those at the beginning of the ten dwellings who keep these precepts, there is the Chapter on Brahma Conduct: examining and contemplating the transcending of marks is precisely the method of keeping these precepts. A beginner who constantly keeps these two chapters will in time naturally accord. As for the abuses mentioned: in the preventive precepts there is the abuse of clinging to marks, and hence of arrogance and self-exaltation and of hating and disparaging those who keep the precepts. Among those who keep the precepts of nature there is the abuse of claiming to have attained what one has not, of indulging oneself and letting feeling run loose, of taking a thief for one's son. Remove these two extremes, and whether one is sharp or dull, one is called a true keeper of the precepts.

Second question, on Chan inquiry: To keep the precepts without according with one's own nature is in the end muddled. To seek to see one's nature, nothing surpasses inquiry. Yet within it doubt and awakening interlock, and the son and the thief are hard to tell apart. I beg you to hand down an enduring mirror, so that I do not fall into the pit of delusion.

Answer: The Buddha spoke of what a renunciant practices: the three studies of precepts, concentration and wisdom. Now the Vinaya is the study of precepts, and inquiry is the study of concentration. But the study of concentration as set out in the teachings is the wondrous gate of the three contemplations, the shortcut to awakening to the mind. Later, when the way of Chan came east, the weight was laid on direct pointing, the single transmission, and seeing one's nature as Chan, without speaking of concentration; yet Chan is concentration. At first Bodhidharma showed the Second Patriarch merely that seeking the mind it is utterly unobtainable, which is called sudden awakening. Even the Sixth Patriarch only taught people not to think of good or evil, and asked which is your own original face; this turning back to seek one's own mind is the work of inquiry. Originally there was no talk of watching a huatou and bringing up doubt. Only later, from Huangbo onward, did people teach the watching of huatous, taking one koan of the ancients as the root of inquiry, and this was transmitted as a literal dharma. Down to the present, masters teach people to inquire into koans only and not to investigate their own minds, and because of this many have been misled. Hence there are many who inquire into Chan today, but none who have gained right knowledge and views; moreover they use Chan inquiry to disparage the teachings, which shows that theirs is not true Chan inquiry. They do not realize that the ancients, because students found it hard to enter, used it as an expedient for a time, wanting only that people recognize their own original mind. How could the buddhas and patriarchs have two minds? They do not realize that raising the huatou, blocking off the root of the intellect, and permitting no arising and ceasing or flowing of a single thought, is precisely the essential gate of entering concentration. People today make of it something strange and special, and so mostly ruin themselves. In inquiry today one cannot do without a huatou, because the beginner's mind is scattered and hard to control and needs this as a handle. Before raising it, one must first steady body and mind, put down inside and outside all at once, put them down until there is nowhere further to put them; then, slowly, muster your strength and raise the huatou, looking back at where it arises — from where does it arise? What after all is it? Because one has not clearly seen one's own mind, one brings up doubt, saying: What is my own original root of life? Seeking thus is called inquiry. One must be undimmed thought after thought and unwavering mind after mind, leaning on it day and night, forgetting sleep and food, until suddenly the bean pops in the cold ashes and the original substance appears before one thought: this is called awakening to one's own mind. When you reach this, you are still just the same person as before, with not the least thing strange about it. If a single thought of joy comes and you take that as enough, that is called taking a thief for your son — how much worse to fabricate all kinds of knowledge and views and utter verses and hymns as rare merchandise? Never fall into this net of māra.

Third question, on koans: After the huatou is shattered, the seventeen hundred tangled vines fall like splitting bamboo. Yet if one case is slightly mistaken, all becomes cloud and fog, and only when the former shattering is undone does one come to believe in the ghost's gate. Not to recognize this fault, but to play with one's spirit and soul, is to lie hidden in the three evil paths.

Answer: If a student can truly see his own mind clearly and reach the place of no doubt, then he breathes through one nostril with the buddhas of the ten directions and the patriarchs of every generation; what need to speak of koans or no koans? This matter is not the business of a beginner; set it aside for now and do not keep it in mind.

Fourth question, on sealing with the teachings: One who does not seal and verify by the teachings does not gain right knowledge and views — this was the Master's former instruction. But the road of conceptual meaning is an old habit, and old habits are hard to dissolve, like oil mixed into flour. If by any chance, in the place of sealing, there is a thread of consciousness, then the awakened one falls instead into skandha-māras, and deviant views are fostered, doing no small harm. I beg you to expose the critical point.

Answer: When the old man ordinarily requires practitioners to seal the mind with the teachings, he means that for what one knows and sees oneself, having never had a clear-eyed person to point out the deviant and the right, one should seal and verify it by the Buddha's sutras. In the Śūraṅgama, the Laṅkāvatāra and the Perfect Enlightenment, what is spoken is all the work of meditation and the essentials of awakening to the mind; one compares one's own mind against them to see whether it accords with what the Buddha said or not. Hence it is said: Take the holy teachings as a bright mirror to illumine one's own mind — not that one takes the mysterious and wondrous phrases of the sutras and turns them into one's own understanding. As for your question, it is precisely that you do not know where the huatou lands. As for the various sicknesses of our mind, only the Buddha has exposed them fully: the rising and sinking of the seven destinies in the Śūraṅgama, the forms of the fifty kinds of skandha-māra, the deviant views of outsiders and the two vehicles in the Laṅkāvatāra. Had the Buddha not spoken in detail, how would we know to fear them? This is what I mean by sealing the mind. One should only illumine the mind by the teachings; it does not consist in the road of conceptual meaning, nor should one take that road as the end. As for old habits of all kinds, they are more than the road of meaning.

Fifth question, on expounding the teachings: The gift of Dharma is great, and the offering of Dharma is supreme. From awakening one seals the teachings, and from that sealing one expounds the teachings; this seems to accord with the Buddha's knowledge and vision and to turn the great Dharma-wheel. Yet if the awakening is not true awakening, one seals by self-confidence; if the sealing is not true sealing, one takes expounding as one's own office, erasing all commentaries and flaunting only one's own clarity. Whether one is a lion or a fox is easy to confuse in oneself; whether one expounds or slanders is hard to know for oneself. I beg you to hand down a precise judgment, and I shall forever consult it as an oracle.

Answer: As a son of the Buddha, one finds the Buddha's grace hard to repay; only by transmitting the Dharma in the Buddha's place is one truly repaying it. Hence among the ancient masters who spread the Dharma there were three kinds. First, those who awakened to their own nature and wondrously accorded with the Buddha's mind, so that the Buddha's words flowed out as if from their own breasts, with the four unhindered eloquence, and who further entered deep into the ocean of the teachings with vast and billowing waves — such as Qingliang, Guifeng and the great patriarchs of Tiantai. Second, those who, though not yet awakened to their own minds, relied on the Buddha's words to seal and settle their minds, broadly exploring the ocean of teachings and expounding as they understood, without erring from the Buddha's intent — such people, though not yet beyond words and images, did not presume to discourse wildly according to their own views but expounded according to the teachings, as the great Dharma-masters of former times. Third, those who had seeds of prajñā from past lives and had the work of meditation, who clarified their own minds and wondrously accorded with the Buddha's intent, but had not broadly engaged in much hearing; their right views were not mistaken. Though they had the fault of taking the shallow for the deep, they had not the crime of slandering the Dharma; what they spread was always with the mind of the gift of Dharma, not seeking worldly fame, profit or respect — such as the venerable Wenling and Jiyin of old. These are all great in the gift of Dharma. As for those who, though clever and of sharp faculties, rely on their own views as attainment, reject ancient and modern alike, let their tongues run wild, and spread the Dharma only for profit — such people not only destroy the Buddhadharma but also mislead and ruin later generations. How could they be called expounders of the Dharma? This is plainly evident and needs no asking.

Sixth question, on versifying the ancients: After awakening, the ancients' verses on the old cases were like painting empty space, not falling into form or mark. People today, whose awakening is not yet thorough, lightly take to versifying the ancients; their lines come from poetic fancy and their repartee resembles buffoonery, yet they take these as words of awakening and states of awakening, and they are on everyone's lips. One turn and they fall into the fox state, and they are placidly unafraid. Is this not a corruption of the Dharma-ending age? We are apt to lose our footing in this pit. I beg you to apply the needle, and I shall everywhere receive your deep compassion.

Answer: Versifying the ancients has existed from of old; it does no more than bring out the ancients' manoeuvres and casually display the arrangements of the house, to manifest the great function and great capacity, and to bring forth one's own hand of letting go and seizing, killing and reviving. It is not merely letting the mouth run and feeling run loose, or composing for the sake of attainment. These two matters, versifying the ancients and expounding the teachings, are not urgent for a beginner; why should one undertake them in advance? The old worthies said: If one but awakens to one's own mind, one need not worry about being unable to expound the Dharma. Thus for a beginner the only urgent thing is to investigate the mind and seek clarity in the great matter of oneself. Never harbor such a view. If we can awaken to our own minds, then even without expounding the teachings or versifying the ancients, ours is a true leaving of home, and we do not disgrace the kāṣāya we wear.
The Dream-Roaming Collection of the Old Man Hanshan, Volume Twelve
Master Jizhao Kai Asks for Instruction on Eight Points

Question: The sutra says that unhindered pure wisdom is born entirely from meditation. How is it then that Nanyue said to Mazu: If you learn sitting meditation, know that Chan is not sitting or lying; if you learn to become a Buddha, know that the Buddha is not a fixed mark. In the Dharma of non-abiding one should not grasp or reject? Which of these two statements is right and which wrong?

Answer: In the patriarchs' gate one does not discuss sitting in meditation or becoming a Buddha; one prizes only seeing one's nature. If one sees one's own nature, clearly and distinctly, there is naturally no grasping or rejecting. The moment there is grasping or rejecting, one falls into right and wrong.

Question: The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: This body of mine is the four great elements — hardness, moisture, warmth and movement — which each return to earth, water, fire and wind; hence it is said that the four elements each separate. Where then is this false body? I do not know whether the elements separate while the body is not yet dead, or separate after death?

Answer: What matters is that before death one can let it go, so that at the time of departure one is not burdened by it. If one waits until the moment itself, to separate is like a live turtle shedding its shell — difficult beyond difficulty. The ancients said: What is done in leisure is used in haste — precisely this.

Question: The Śūraṅgama Sūtra says that Ānanda asked the Buddha: In the road of the original arousal of the mind, from what does one gather and subdue it, to enter the Buddha's knowledge and vision? The Buddha said: If you wish to enter the Buddha's knowledge and vision, you should examine carefully whether the mind aroused on the causal ground is the same as or different from the enlightenment of the fruit ground. If on the causal ground one takes the mind of arising and ceasing as the ground of practice and yet seeks the Buddha Vehicle's non-arising and non-ceasing, there is no such possibility. I do not know whether the mind with which one now inquires into Chan and studies the Way in order to escape birth and death is a mind of arising and ceasing.

Answer: When a student inquires into Chan, he first cuts off the mind of arising and ceasing; when it becomes clear, he then sees the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing. If one inquires with a mind of arising and ceasing, one merely follows deluded thoughts in their flow; that is not inquiry.

Question: Chan Master Baizhang Huaihai said: To visit good teachers and seek a bit of knowledge or half an understanding is the māra of the good teacher, because it gives rise to views of words. To make the four great vows, vowing to save all beings and only then become a Buddha, is the māra of the wisdom of the bodhisattva Dharma, because one does not let go of the vow. To keep fasts and precepts and cultivate meditation and learning and wisdom is a root of good with outflows; even if one sits on the bodhi seat and attains perfect enlightenment and saves beings numerous as Ganges sands, all realizing the fruit of pratyekabuddha, it is the māra of good roots, because one gives rise to greed and clinging. If toward all dharmas one has no greed or defilement, and the principle of Chan alone remains, with most profound meditation and no further advance, that is the māra of samādhi, because one long indulges and plays in it. How can one who now inquires into Chan and studies the Way escape these māras and enter the right road of practice?
Answer: All practitioners, simply because their mental views are not forgotten, move along with the net of māra. If mental views are dissolved and forgotten, then even the Buddha is not established.
Question: In breaking the clinging to the four elements and the five aggregates, is there a before and after?

Answer: The teachings say that the five aggregates are broken gradually and that the form aggregate must be broken first. But if in Chan inquiry one smashes the lacquer bucket, then the consciousness aggregate is broken first. Once the consciousness aggregate is broken, the four elements have no support, and so it is like cutting water or blowing on light — no contact at all.

Question: As for the four phrases of the Diamond Sūtra, from ancient times to now no one has spoken of them clearly. Some point to form, sound, scent and the like as the four phrases; some point to eye, ear, nose and tongue; some to all marks being non-marks; some to the truth of existence and the truth of non-existence. As for Vasubandhu, he said: I ascended to the Tuṣita heaven and asked Maitreya for instruction, and he said: No mark of self, no mark of a person, no mark of a being, no mark of a life. The Sixth Patriarch said: Mahāprajñāpāramitā. And Master Shanhui of Shuanglin said again: Holding the four phrases in the sutra, one should not be apart from one's body; the foolish see it as a dream, the wise see only the real. From ancient times to the present there has never been a settled wording — why is this?

Answer: The Buddha's teaching of prajñā is like the many herbs of the snowy mountains: every one of them is medicine, and picked up and used it will certainly cure the illness. So when the ancients pointed out what the four phrases are, each was plucking one stalk of grass from the snowy mountains.

Question: The ancients said: Even when one reaches utter purity without a speck, it is still the outflow of true permanence. Even when one reaches the point where not one dharma stands before the mind, one is still subject to Yangshan's inspection. Even when one reaches the state where the whole body is illumination, one is still within the monk's letting down of the hand. Even when one realizes that which is before the seven buddhas and beyond Sound-Voice, it is still a matter of understanding words. Do students today really reach these states?

Answer: The ancients' handed-down words were only out of fear that people would fall by the roadside. Even if a student reaches this, it is still a matter of the roadside; how much more so, not having reached it, to open one's mouth and talk of Chan — that is always deceiving one's own mind.

Question: Master Yuanwu said: Since there have been patriarchs, their sole concern has been the single transmission and direct pointing: using words to drive out words, using the mechanism to seize the mechanism, using poison to attack poison, using function to break function. Hence the branches and schools divided, each mastering its own style. One must be of supreme faculties and have the will to perpetuate and prosper the buddhas and patriarchs; only then can one enter deeply into the inner chamber and only then be sealed and verified. Apart from this, one should treasure and keep it secret and not take it lightly. Now I see students who mostly do not examine their own faculties but want to inquire into the matter above. Is faculty truly not to be discussed?

Answer: The patriarchs' selection of people takes faculties into account; this is the same as the Buddha's discussion of lineages in the teachings. If one is not of such a lineage, one remains stuck to skin and bone. People today, whose faculties are impure, are certainly wholly excluded from this matter. If one is willing to give one's mind to this matter and from then on not retreat, in time one may be permitted to advance. Such a one falls within the category of the undetermined lineage.
