Question: The Buddha taught the sudden teaching and the gradual teaching, and Chan opened the sudden gate and the gradual gate. These two teachings and two gates — are they the same or different?

Answer: When the buddhas and patriarchs appeared in the world, they fundamentally had no dharma to speak. And since the Dharma is fundamentally without speech, how could there be distinctions of sudden and gradual? The talk of sudden and gradual is set up solely for the sake of faculties and has nothing to do with the Dharma. Now as to the teachings having sudden and gradual: when Vairocana first attained perfect enlightenment and at the site of bodhi taught the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, he suddenly revealed the gate of the mind-ground of the equal dharma-realm, directly showing it without remainder, like the sun newly risen that first illumines the high mountains. Those who later classified the teachings called it the perfect and sudden gate; this is the Buddha's sudden Dharma. Yet this sudden Dharma was bestowed only on one class of beings of great faculties on the grounds; within it the forty-two stages are arranged — that is the gradual within the sudden. The remaining beings of inferior faculties in the assembly were as blind and deaf, wholly excluded. Thus, though the Dharma was great, the faculties it gathered were not broad; it is what is called there being only one gate, and that one narrow. Would the Buddha teach the Dharma for one person alone? Therefore he manifested response bodies and transformation bodies, established according to the three kinds of faculties, and taught the three vehicles' dharmas, beginning with gradual cultivation and realization — what is called the gradual of the teachings. Later, in the Laṅkāvatāra, the Lotus and the Nirvāṇa, he suddenly revealed the seed of buddha-nature; this is the sudden coming from the gradual. This is how the teachings are divided into sudden and gradual. As for the one gate of Chan, it is spoken of everywhere in the teachings. Among the bodhisattva's six pāramitās there are the two of meditation and wisdom; the classifying of the bodhisattva teachings opens from these two the two gates of calming and contemplation as the ground of practice. Here the teaching uses the sudden while cultivating gradually, so that Chan is the gradual within the sudden. As for Bodhidharma's Chan: it was the World-Honored One's holding up of the flower at the end, and Mahākāśyapa's breaking into a smile; the Buddha then showed him the treasury of the true Dharma-eye and the wondrous mind of nirvāṇa, and so it became the purport of the special transmission outside the teachings. Twenty-eight transmissions in the Western regions, then Bodhidharma came east, and six transmissions to Caoxi; and the patriarchs recorded below in the Transmission of the Lamp are the Chan of the single transmission directly pointing to the one mind, which cannot be compared with the Chan of the six pāramitās. For this singly shows the one mind and no other dharma, directly seeing one's own mind at once, not belonging to cultivation, realization, delusion, awakening, cause or fruit; it specially reveals the one point of the Buddha before he appeared in the world. This is called the path above, and named the sudden teaching of the Great Vehicle. This is the sudden of Chan. As for the patriarchs of every generation who suddenly awakened to this mind: though it be under a single word or phrase, a single blow or shout, they awakened directly — this is because of practice through many lives, with deep roots of prajñā, when causes and conditions ripened and matured today; there are also those who in this life inquire for twenty or thirty years before they awaken. Thus, though sudden, it also comes from the gradual. As Weishan said: If a student can in a single thought awaken clearly to his own mind and recognize what he originally possesses, this is called awakening; yet there still remain beginningless ignorance and subtle outflows, and so with what he has awakened he purifies the outflowing consciousness of present karma, and this is called cultivation; there is no other cultivation apart from this. Seen thus, within the sudden there is never a lack of the gradual. I have observed that the Laṅkāvatāra divides sudden and gradual into four gates: first, sudden-sudden; second, sudden-gradual; third, gradual-sudden; fourth, gradual-gradual. Know from this that one cannot hold to one and speak of all. Though one awakens suddenly, gradual cultivation is not abandoned; the minds of the buddhas and patriarchs are from the first not two.

Question: The Buddha's various sutras are all talks according with nature and purport of definitive meaning. Why is it that Bodhidharma praised the Laṅkāvatāra repeatedly, saying, This sutra is the essence of my mind, while Huangmei pointed to the Diamond? What difference is there in the other sutras?

Answer: The Buddha's various Mahāyāna sutras, though they are talks according with nature and of definitive meaning, in their gate of establishing conversion do not depart from delusion and awakening and from the mutual opposition of nature and characteristics; they insist on returning from the false to the real, and all have their harmonizing before the one real is revealed. As for the Laṅkāvatāra, it directly points to the one mind. Though it speaks of the real and the false, it shows that the storehouse of consciousness is itself the tathāgatagarbha, and no harmonizing is needed; it reveals only the state of the holy wisdom of self-awakening. One need only understand that the deluded thoughts manifested by one's own mind are without nature, and that is holy wisdom; no further turning is required. As for its practice, one simply contemplates directly the flowing of one's own mind and the present measure of deluded thought, and penetrates one's own mind at once, without establishing stages or ranks. Hence those who classify the teachings name it the gate of the sudden teaching. Therefore Bodhidharma took it as the mind-seal, using this sutra to show the essential key of the Chan school; and because this sutra is hard to understand and difficult for inferior understanding to enter, when the transmission reached Huangmei he used the Diamond to seal the mind. The Diamond is one of the eight divisions of prajñā, whose text runs to six hundred scrolls; only this scroll alone accords with the patriarchs' mind-seal. For prajñā is the initial gate of entering the Great Vehicle, exactly as the Śūraṅgama says: the bodhisattva takes the mind of non-arising and non-ceasing as the ground of practice. And prajñā is the Buddha's fundamental real wisdom, which is precisely the mind of non-arising and non-ceasing. This sutra takes non-abiding as its principle and the cutting off of doubt as its function. Because the two vehicles falsely give rise to views of beings, of a Buddha and of dharmas, and to all kinds of abiding and clinging, and bring up doubt layer upon layer, this sutra plucks out the root of doubt entirely and brings one to the place of no doubt, where knowledge and views perish and not one dharma is established, dispelling all clinging minds. This is exactly the same as the Chan school's method of loosening the glue and removing the bonds, cutting off the discriminations of intellect and words — precisely the Chan school's not permitting deliberation, not attaching to thought, withering consciousness and emotion, and penetrating above the dharmakāya. Hence Huangmei's sealing the mind with this sutra was well founded. The other sutras all have some stickiness; this sutra alone is clean-cutting. If one understands this in Chan inquiry, one enters easily.

Question: It is said that there is Tathāgata Chan and patriarch Chan. Do these two Chans really have sameness or difference? When Xiangyan, on hearing the pebble strike the bamboo, had an awakening, he presented to Yangshan the verse beginning Last year's poverty was not yet true poverty. Yangshan said: I am glad that my brother understands Tathāgata Chan, but patriarch Chan — you have not yet dreamed of it. By these words one sees that Tathāgata Chan and patriarch Chan are different. Yet if from Mahākāśyapa it was transmitted to the First Patriarch who came from the West, and patriarch succeeded patriarch, the first patriarch of all the schools is Śākyamuni himself — how could there be any difference?

Answer: Tathāgata Chan and patriarch Chan are from the first not two. Only, Tathāgata Chan speaks of awakening within delusion and requires cultivation before entering; patriarch Chan directly points to the one point that does not belong to delusion or awakening and does not depend on cultivation, requiring a person to awaken at once to his own mind directly. Whoever falls into the juncture of delusion and awakening is already in the secondary meaning. Hence the old worthy said: Cultivation is indeed not absent — but what of defilement? Therefore the Chan school's path above requires one who is a man of that ilk before one can attain it. Among the four kinds of Chan in the Laṅkāvatāra, the supreme one-vehicle Chan is precisely patriarch Chan. In truth there is from the first no difference. If one's faculties are impure and one recklessly flaunts cleverness and knowledge and views, taking that as understanding patriarch Chan, then one has not even dreamed of Tathāgata Chan. It is like a poor man falsely claiming to be a king and bringing execution upon himself. Should one not fear it? Should one not fear it?
Instruction to Xiao Xuanpu, Minister of Rites (from the sixth day of the tenth month in the winter of the guihai year of the Tianqi era, his brush here fell still)

In entering the Way one must first awaken clearly to the mind-substance of this person, which is from the beginning luminous and vast, embracing all without exclusion, filled and pure, in which saint and ordinary are not established and which is not confined or obstructed by body, mind or world. This is the path above, the mind-seal of the coming from the West — this and nothing more. Once one can awaken thoroughly to this mind, then in daily life, responding to conditions, all states are like images in a mirror: nothing sticks when they come, no trace remains when they go. In this way whatever one does flows out from the true mind and the real, and each act is a true and deathless undertaking — one that not only vies in brightness with the sun and moon. Compared with the petty contrivances of deluded people's deluded thoughts and schemes, how can it be mentioned in the same breath? This radiance is complete in everyone, from the first without lack. But because the view of self is firm, whatever one does one takes as one's own merit and holds one's own view to be certainly right; right and wrong interlace, and in the end there is no settled conclusion. The reason for this is that without a mind vast and greatly impartial, one wishes to establish an undertaking that will not decay for a thousand autumns — that is hard indeed.

Our mind-substance is from the beginning perfect and luminous; that we cannot now awaken suddenly nor enjoy it before us is because through measureless kalpas greed, anger, delusion and craving and all kinds of affliction have obstructed and covered our own minds. Hence the work of gradual cultivation cannot be dispensed with. Weishan said: If a student can in a single thought suddenly awaken to his own mind, he has only to take what he has awakened and purify the outflowing consciousness of present karma; this is called cultivation, and there is no other cultivation apart from this. If a student of the Way seeks only sudden awakening as the end and supposes there is no work to do, then his habits lie deep and secretly break out when he meets conditions, and in time he flows into the realm of māra. Yet the work of gradual cultivation is also without stages: in daily life, at the place where a thought has not yet stirred, plant your feet firmly and turn the gaze inward; at the place where a thought arises, pursue and examine that thought — from where does it arise? Pursue it to the place where the thought arises and find that it was from the first unborn; then all deluded thoughts and feelings melt like ice on the spot. What is to be avoided is lacking the power of bravery, so that one cannot grip the throat and, unaware, lets it continue, and so flows on and never returns.
Instruction to Zhou Ziyin (the following is appended from Haiyin's drafts)

Today in the mountain dwelling the assembly begins its retreat, and Haiyin takes the seat to expound the Lotus Sūtra. At that moment your handwritten letter arrived, along with fine fruit. This is enough to divine that you too are a man of the Dharma assembly, one who has already attained the fruit of the Way. This is no earthenware divination. What your former letter said, and my daily practice, are exactly in accord; you may also gradually enter the gate of non-duality. But in your daily life, every matter and every thought is a mind of arising and ceasing; how can you take quiescent extinction as joy? If you seek a measure of benefit in the mind-ground, you must all the more, when your reading and writing are done, at every place where you meet conditions, be firmly grounded on the spot and suddenly turn the gaze inward, contemplating where these various doings and this mind of arising and ceasing arise from, and where they now cease. Contemplating deeply thus for a long time, you will gradually enter into subtlety and closeness. Further, wherever the habits secretly flow and afflictions arise without cause, look steadily and firmly at it: see what it finally is and where it arises and ceases. Pursue it to the place where its traces are swept away and extinguished — like dropping a flake of snow into a cauldron of boiling water. In daily life thus, not a thought may be let go. The moment the least thought of laziness, sloth or indolence arises, the mind that seeks ease and comfort and enjoyment — that is precisely the root of the illness breaking out. Then at once raise your eyebrows and glare; do not let it bind you. The moment you see the binding, never let yourself fall over with it and roll about with it in the dust. Most strictly avoid this. For the most part, one invocation of a bodhisattva or one invocation of a Buddha, clung to with desperate urgency, is what you press against it with. When various evil habits arise, then with all your strength raise up this huatou and swing it at the sky: no matter whether it be māra or Buddha, affliction or habit, good or evil deliberation, all the dust of feeling is cut off at once, like slicing through tangled silk. Doing the work thus, it does not hinder your reading or your writing. As for reading, see where the book you read is lodged; as for writing, see from where that writing flows. Nor does it hinder receiving guests and entertaining visitors, drinking tea and eating rice, or relieving oneself. In every place there is no need of the slightest crack or gap. Settle your mind thus. Then compare it with what Yongjia said: Just when the mind is applied, precisely no mind is applied; no mind precisely applies, constantly applying yet precisely nothing. Is this the same or not the same? I do not know whether you can believe the old man Haiyin and not be deceived. Try it and see for yourself. If you find the faith not mistaken, then you will know how very laughable Yan Hui's three months of fasting the mind was. As for the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment, read it until familiar and take it as your daily lesson morning and evening, and when we meet in the spring we shall decide it together. My ordinary letters to you inevitably carry a little emotion and consciousness; I am ashamed that I have not brought you to thorough penetration. It is not that I am not thorough; I fear that your faith is not thorough. Now I see your faith gradually increasing and drawing daily nearer purity. If at this moment I do not cut out this bare heart and give it to you, when will you be thorough? If you dawdle and are not thorough, then Haiyin will go on being thorough by himself. What do you say? What do you say? The human world is pitiable; this Way is pitiable; but the mind I hope for in you is more pitiable still.

Your letter asking for instruction is most sincere and earnest. But you have not yet got the two words empty and illusory exactly right, and hence there is obstruction in regard to mind and objects, which is why the work is hard to do. Now I shall speak it out plainly for you, and then it will be clear and you will have no further doubt. What is called empty is not the emptiness of utter nothingness; it is like the vulgar saying, as if there were no one beside him — could it be that there really is no one beside him? It is only that, raised high in his eyes, there is no such person. What is called illusory is not the illusory of weird transformations; it means existing yet not real. It is like a conjuror at a fair pulling many figures out of a tube: the tube contains nothing at all, yet suddenly there they are; though they exist, they are not real. Since they are not real, they are fundamentally not there; because they are fundamentally not there, it is said to be empty. Hence it is said: It is like a conjured man — it is not that there is no conjured man, but the conjured man is not a real man. Since the man is not real, is he not empty? The Buddha's word empty was spoken to break the world's clinging to things as truly existing; it does not mean utter nothingness and annihilation. Truly fearing that people of the world would sink into annihilation, he spoke further the word illusory to dispel their view of annihilation. Thus all dharmas of body and mind are empty because illusory, and because empty they are said to be like illusions. Observing these two words as depending on each other, one at once sees their wonder. What is called empty is contemplating emptiness by way of illusory existence, and is named true emptiness; what is called existence is the illusory existence of what is fundamentally not there, and is named wondrous existence. Because of true emptiness the mind is not annihilated; because of wondrous existence objects are unborn. Since objects are unborn, what can the mind grasp? Since the mind is not annihilated, how can deluded thoughts remain? If deluded thoughts do not remain, with what mind will one grasp objects? Objects are themselves illusory; with what objects will they pull the mind? Thus the mind does not grasp objects, yet the mind is not annihilated; objects do not pull the mind, yet objects are just as they are. When mind and objects are thus, wherein is one not joyful? This is what is meant by: The mind is fundamentally unborn and exists because of objects; if the objects before it were absent, the mind too would be absent. One need only see through their illusory unreality and call it as if absent; then the numinous mind shines alone and the deluded mind suddenly rests, and that is called also absent. What is absent is the deluded mind — how could the true mind be utterly absent? What is the deluded mind? It is the one that clings to objects without dissolving. What is the true mind? It is the one that does not grasp the marks of body, mind or objects, that clearly and constantly knows, numinous and silently illumining. Applying the mind thus, what obstruction is there? Hence it is said: When the mind grasps the mind itself, the non-illusory becomes illusory dharmas; when there is no grasping, there is nothing that is not illusory; since even the non-illusory does not arise, how can illusory dharmas stand? It is precisely as said: Objects and conditions have no beauty or ugliness; beauty and ugliness arise from the mind. If the mind does not forcibly name them, how can love and hate arise? Thus, if feeling does not adhere to things, how can things obstruct a person? Since things cannot obstruct a person, how can a person obstruct things? The reason people of the world have no freedom is only that they do not understand that mind and objects are unborn and unreal, like illusions. If one understands that a single thought is unborn and like an illusion, then all suffering and joy, care and trouble, gain and loss, love and hate, grasping and rejecting, melt and dissolve like ice on the spot. Hence it is said: Knowing the illusory, one at once departs, without using expedients; departing from the illusory, one is at once awake, and there are no stages. This is what is meant by reaching the Buddha's house in a single thought — no empty saying. You have only to observe that wherever deluded thoughts arise and cease, wherever states arise and cease, they are nothing but illusory and unreal; then the mind will naturally not run after objects, and objects will naturally not pull the mind. Coming and going, responding to conditions, one thought is empty and bright, numinous and shining alone, illumining the body and mind before one as illusory and conjured, like the moon in water, like an image in a mirror, like a cloud in the sky, like the shimmering of heat waves. Holding it thus with the vajra eye, move it no more. Let whatever states come — touched, they dissolve; let whatever deluded mind come — glanced at, it perishes. Applying the mind thus, what delusion is there that could trouble you? What deluded state could assail your mind? These words are Haiyin's utmost, laying himself bare wholly for you and overturning everything to the bottom. Do not doubt further. Above all, do not think ahead and reckon behind; all such deliberation is evil perception and evil habit, and all of it is a cause that obstructs the Way. If you follow this old man's words, you are this moment a man of the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Writing freely as the brush comes, I have not noticed how clumsily I have babbled; such a grandmotherly heart, leaking and dripping thus. Take care.

It is several months since we parted, all in a blur; the flowing light is swift and the sun and moon cheat one. Whenever I hear that you are twice as diligent as usual, joy pours into and irrigates my mind-field. At first I intended that after your honored father had gone, you would surely come into the mountains for a meeting, so that we might seal and verify your past work and decide it together. This hope was so real that it took shape in a dream — laughable, that a man of the Way should fall into such sentiment and views. Your letter says: By sitting I seek stillness; by stillness I seek the mind. This is the initial gate of entering the Way and is most apt. But within sitting you have not yet understood the crucial point; hence you grow weary from sitting long. Because you have not penetrated the wonder of the mind-substance, after being still for long you wish for some news; and you are also doubtful and adrift, as if with nowhere to return. It is truly because the mind that seeks has not obtained the secret key, and so the very thought of seeking feels instead like toil. Thus you seek the mind with the mind — exactly like a thirsty deer chasing the heat shimmer. The transmission says: Knowing where to rest, one then attains stability. Because your mind does not yet know where to rest, you do not attain stability. You ask for a list of methods for governing the mind, such as the four noes and the three reflections, to lead this mind in and hold this mind steady. This is where your refined and bitter earnestness lies, and it is what I greatly hope for in you. Now that you are willing to pledge yourself in your own heart, how could I instead be secretive and stingy? My only fear is that you, having begun in our Buddhadharma without having heard much, may in the midst of its names and phrases mostly turn them into the stale habits of your former seeing and hearing, so that the medicine of ambrosia cannot take effect near at hand in restoring your countenance. The methods by which the buddhas and patriarchs of old taught people, though their roads are many, do not go beyond the three studies of precepts, concentration and wisdom — what is called: from precepts arises concentration, from concentration arises wisdom. As for the detail of their items, among the sutras none surpasses the Śūraṅgama; as for the patriarchs' words, none surpass the single book of Yongjia's Collection. Read it until familiar and savor it. As for the key to entering concentration and applying the mind in it, as it says: Just when the mind is applied, precisely no mind is applied; no mind precisely applies, constantly applying yet precisely nothing. And again: After conditions are forgotten, still and silent; the nature of numinous knowing, clear and distinct; in the darkness of dull blankness, brightly shining; according with fundamental true emptiness, perfectly certain. This is the divine talisman for applying the mind. As for the four noes and the three reflections, these are precisely the precepts; all is contained therein. In truth the items of the work of cultivating the mind do not go beyond the three gates of calming, contemplation and even holding. In that Collection, śamatha is calming; vipaśyanā is contemplation; and yuganaddha is the twin operation of calming and contemplation and the even holding of concentration and wisdom. Let this serve for now to answer your request. The passages circled in red in the Collection — give them your attention for news of the matter. If there is anything you do not understand, do not hesitate to send questions again and again. As for the shortcut method of calming and contemplation, allow me to write another page later, to make up for today's deficit.
